paper.title: Follistatin regulates tooth root furcation morphogenesis.
paper.journal: The International journal of developmental biology
paper.abstract: Follistatin (Fst), an extracellular inhibitor of the TGF-β signaling pathway, plays a critical role in tooth development, particularly in crown morphogenesis and enamel patterning. While molar root number is conserved within species and between upper and lower jaws, the molecular mechanisms governing root patterning remain largely unknown. To investigate the role of Fst in root formation, we analyzed K14-Cre-mediated Fst knockout mice. During embryonic and early postnatal stages, Fst was dynamically expressed in the dental epithelium including the lingual epithelium, and primary and secondary enamel knots, as well as in the dental mesenchyme at the base of the dental papilla. However, during root formation, Fst expression became restricted to the outer layer of Hertwig's epithelial root sheath (HERS). Micro-CT analysis revealed that mutant mice exhibited molar root abnormalities, including enlarged pulp chambers and partial furcation defects on the lingual side of the mandibular molars. Histological analysis showed that, while HERS initially exhibited buccolingual asymmetry - with the buccal-side HERS extending more prominently in both control and mutant mice - control mice eventually established bucco-lingual symmetry in HERS extension, ensuring proper root furcation formation. In contrast, mutant mice displayed delayed lingual-side HERS extension, resulting in defective root furcation. Molecular analysis revealed that Gli1 expression was upregulated, whereas Cdkn1a and Wnt signaling molecules (Wnt4, Lhx6, and Notum) were significantly downregulated in the delayed lingual HERS of mutant mice. These findings suggest that Fst regulates tooth root morphogenesis by modulating Shh and Wnt signaling to control lingual epithelial proliferation and HERS extension. This study offers novel insights into the molecular mechanisms governing molar root number and morphology determination.

paper.title: Notch-hedgehog antagonism regulates stem cell niche formation through an E2-E3-E3 ubiquitin module.
paper.abstract: Distinct microenvironments, including the stem cell niche and differentiation zone, promote stem cell self-renewal and progeny differentiation, yet how these domains are established remains unclear. In the developing Drosophila ovary, we show that Notch activation silences Hedgehog (Hh) signaling in anterior intermingled cells (ICs), specifying cap cells (CpCs) that form the germline stem cell (GSC) niche. Notch upregulates the E2 enzyme Ubc10, which partners with the RBR E3 ligase Ari-1 and a Cullin 3 (Cul3)-based RING E3 ligase to assemble an E2-E3-E3 complex, targeting Ci for degradation. By contrast, ICs posterior to CpCs retain Hh signaling and give rise to escort cells, forming the GSC differentiation zone. ARIH1, CUL3, and GLI2, the human orthologs of Ari-1, Cul3, and Ci, associate in human cells, suggesting conservation of this ubiquitin ligase module. Together, these findings identify a Notch-dependent E2-E3-E3 ubiquitin ligase module linking Notch activation to Hh silencing during niche patterning. This strategy may act broadly in cell-fate decisions and reveals a paradigm in which a developmental cue regulates an E2 enzyme to facilitate ubiquitin ligase assembly.

paper.title: Brushite-modified titanium surface elicits early osteointegrative gene expression signatures in human mesenchymal stem cells: insights from NGS analysis.
paper.abstract: Brushite (dicalcium phosphate dihydrate) is a resorbable coating with significant potential to enhance implant osseointegration. However, the early molecular mechanisms through which it directs mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) behavior remain poorly understood. This study investigates the early transcriptional response of human MSCs cultured on brushite-coated Ti6Al4V compared to uncoated titanium at 7 days, a critical regulatory window that precedes overt differentiation. By employing both basal and osteogenic culture conditions, we decoupled material-specific effects from soluble biochemical cues. ICP-OES confirmed a high-purity Ca/P-based coating. RNA-seq analysis identified 390 and 613 differentially expressed genes under osteogenic and basal conditions, respectively, demonstrating a robust material-driven response. Pathway enrichment revealed the selective involvement of pro-osteogenic signaling (BMP, Wnt, Hedgehog), metabolic/mitochondrial reprogramming, and a controlled inflammatory response. Conversely, the downregulation of proliferation- and mechanotransduction-related genes is consistent with a transition toward a stabilized, differentiation-permissive state. Notably, a 25-gene core signature was identified across all conditions, representing a stable material-dependent transcriptional fingerprint. These findings were validated by qRT-PCR and corroborated at the protein level via multiplex assays (Bio-Plex), showing increased secretion of extracellular matrix and pro-regenerative factors. Collectively, our findings suggest that brushite is not merely a passive scaffold but promotes an early transcriptional program in MSCs consistent with osteogenic commitment, highlighting its potential to accelerate the clinical performance of bioactive implants.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Titanium implants, widely used in orthopedic and dental applications, offer excellent biocompatibility and mechanical properties. However, their ability to achieve osseointegration, i.e., the bond between the implant and bone tissue, is strongly influenced by the surface characteristics. Surface modification tailors the implant interface to optimize biological interactions and promote efficient osseointegration (Bagno et al., 2004; Abdo et al., 2025).

Key surface modification techniques include: 1) Surface roughening (mechanical methods like sandblasting or chemical methods like acid etching), which increases surface area for cells attachment, improving bone-implant contact; 2) Metallic coatings (e.g. welded beads, mesh, plasma spray coatings), mainly made of titanium, which create a rougher surface and eventually a layer with interconnected pores, ideal for long-term fixation; 3) Coating with bioactive materials (e.g., hydroxyapatite, brushite, or calcium phosphates), which mimic bone mineral components and enhance biological activity; 4) Anodization and plasma electrolytic oxidation, which create a thicker, nano-structured oxide layer to promote cells adhesion and can be functionalized for further bioactivity; 5) Hydrophilic treatments, which make the surface water-attractive, improving protein adsorption and cells attachment (Wu et al., 2025; Le Guéhennec et al., 2007; Xue et al., 2020). These modifications are critical for promoting osseointegration, the direct bond between living bone and the implant, which is essential for the long-term success of orthopedic, dental, and spinal implants Successful osseointegration requires biocompatible, non-toxic surfaces that actively support bone cell adhesion, differentiation, and integration. (Zhu et al., 2021; Novaes et al., 2010; Hao et al., 2021). Surface modification is therefore crucial to enhance bone healing and implant stability while reducing fibrous tissue formation, implant loosening, inflammation, infection, and overall implant failure (Zhu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025; Hotchkiss et al., 2016; Boyan et al., 2016). Ongoing research aims to clarify how surface roughness, coatings, chemical composition, and wettability influence the behavior of mesenchymal cells and osteoblasts, including cell adhesion, proliferation, differentiation, and matrix formation (Boyan et al., 2016). Key molecular signaling pathways, such as growth factor–and integrin-mediated signaling, are being studied for their roles in osseointegration. However, the molecular basis of these responses remains largely unresolved, and surface modifications may modulate multiple biological pathways that influence the healing process. Additionally, while surface modifications often improve short-term osseointegration, their long-term effects remain uncertain. The lack of understanding of these mechanisms has led to empirical approaches in implant design, creating challenges in optimizing treatments and predicting outcomes. Therefore, while surface modification is critical to the success of titanium implants, the biological and molecular mechanisms underlying osseointegration remain complex and incompletely comprehended. Continued research is required to elucidate these mechanisms and to guide the optimization of implant design for safer, more effective, and more durable orthopedic devices. Among the surface modifications of greatest interest due to its biological characteristics and strong interaction with the surrounding tissue is electrochemically deposited dicalcium phosphate dihydrate, or brushite. This method is commonly used as a coating in orthopedic and dental implants due to its advantages over hydroxyapatite (HA) thermal spray coatings. These benefits include higher solubility, which releases more Ca2 and PO3 at the implant interface, lower-temperature production, and a non-line-of-sight application method that enables uniform coating of irregularly shaped implants (Ducheyne et al., 1993). Also, the application method based on electrochemical deposition is ideal for “complex” surfaces like those obtained by Additive Manufacturing, which can have intricate geometries and porosity where traditional (line-of-sight) coatings fail (Wu et al., 2025; Le Guéhennec et al., 2007; Xue et al., 2020). Brushite resorbs faster than HA, making it well suited for temporary surgical applications where controlled resorption supports healing and tissue integration. In bone repair, brushite-coated implants resorb more quickly, providing early mechanical support while enabling gradual replacement by native bone. As the material dissolves, new bone fills the space, allowing brushite to function as a temporary scaffold rather than a permanent implant (Lukina et al., 2023; Tamimi et al., 2008; Reigstad et al., 2007). This is particularly useful in cases such as bone fracture repair or bone defect regeneration, where the implant helps guide the healing process. Once healing progresses, the material resorbs, minimizing the long-term presence of foreign material. This process helps avoid issues like chronic inflammation, immune responses, or implant failure, which are more likely if the implant remains in the body permanently. The rapid resorption of brushite also lowers the risk of complications such as infection or loosening, as the material disappears once the healing process is complete. Additionally, as brushite resorbs, it promotes bone remodeling by creating a dynamic environment where new bone gradually replaces the material. In contrast, non-resorbable materials such as HA may sustain this process to a lesser extent, potentially influencing bone remodelling once healing is complete. Again, while the benefits of brushite coatings in promoting osseointegration are well established, the molecular and biological mechanisms driving these effects, such as specific cellular interactions, signaling pathways, and bone remodeling processes, are still not fully understood. This gap in knowledge presents a challenge, as deeper understanding is essential for further optimizing biocompatibility and performances of implants.

This study aims to address this gap in the current state of research and highlights the need for continued investigation to fully elucidate these processes. In our previous study (Raimondi et al., 2025), we showed that brushite-coated Ti6Al4V enhances bone healing and osseointegration by modulating the secretome of human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), selected for their multipotency, homing ability, and immunomodulatory functions. Brushite promoted the secretion of osteogenic factors, proteins involved in blood clotting, energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, stress responses, and chromatin-related proteins, suggesting a role for chromatin dynamics in bone regeneration (Raimondi et al., 2025). These findings identify brushite-coated Ti6Al4V as a promising scaffold for bone regeneration and warrant further investigation of its molecular mechanisms. While secretome analysis reveals protein-level changes, next-generation sequencing (NGS) provides a broader view of the transcriptional programs and pathways driving these responses. Integrating both approaches enables a comprehensive understanding of how brushite-coated titanium regulates regenerative signaling and functional protein expression. Here, we performed next-generation sequencing (NGS) of MSCs cultured for 7 days on brushite-coated or uncoated Ti6Al4V under both osteogenic and basal conditions to distinguish the effects of soluble differentiation cues from the intrinsic bioactivity of the brushite coating. The 7-day time point was selected to capture the early molecular events preceding overt osteogenic differentiation. Key osteogenic markers were validated by qRT-PCR, and Bio-Plex/Luminex assays assessed the corresponding protein changes. Overall, our findings reveal coordinated early transcriptional responses showing that brushite actively directs MSC commitment toward osseointegrative lineages rather than acting as a passive scaffold.

Preparation of substrates
The specimen substrates (diameter 10 mm, thickness 3 mm) were fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) at Lincotek Medical facility (Italy), using a M290 machine (EOS GmbH, Germany) equipped with a 400 W laser source. These specimens were fabricated from a biomedical grade titanium alloy (Ti6Al4V) powder with particle sizes ranging from 15 to 45 μm (Ti64ELI, EOS GmbH, Germany). After fabrication, all specimens were subjected to a vacuum heat treatment to transform the initial α′-martensitic microstructure into a stable α+β phase, thereby relieving the residual stresses generated during the L-PBF process. Finally, the native AM surface was cleaned with a mixture of distilled water and commercial tetrasodium pyrophosphate (M 30, FIMM SAS, France).

Brushite electrodeposition process
The coatings were deposited by a pulsed cathodic galvanostatic technique at Lincotek Medical facility (Italy) using the Ti6Al4V disc as the cathode and a platinum-coated titanium mesh as the anode, immersed in a supersaturated calcium phosphate aqueous solution obtained by dissolving calcium phosphate monobasic monohydrate (Sigma Aldrich-Merck, Germany) in distilled water (30 g/L).

The electrolyte provides an electrical circuit between the electrodes in the cell. The deposition occurs under a pulsed electrical current (Raimondi et al., 2025).

During electrodeposition, the reactions described by the Equations 1-5 may occur at the surface of the cathode submerged in the electrolytic solution. O2+2H2O+4e−→4OH− (1) 2H2O+2e−→H2+2OH− (2) 2H++2e−→H2 (3) H2PO4−+OH−→HPO42−+H2 (4) HPO4−+OH−→PO43−+H2 (5)

Equation 2 corresponds to the reduction of H2O which results in formation of hydrogen bubbles near the working electrode. As hydrogen is one of the products of Equations 2, 3, the local pH of the electrolyte solution in the vicinity of the cathode increases. The increased pH level provides a suitable substrate for acid–base reactions, as stated in Equation 4. An increase in concentration of OH- ions can lead to the increased number of hydrogen phosphate and phosphate ions through Equations 4, 5, i.e., reduction reactions of HPO4 2- and PO4 3-.

Ions present in the electrolyte, such as Ca2+ and H+, move toward the cathode due to the electric field gradient, while existing HPO4 2- ions remain in the diffusing layer due to the differential concentration between the surface of cathode and the bulk electrolyte. Figure 1 schematically illustrates the movement of the main ions toward the cathode during electrodeposition.

On the surface of the cathode, calcium ions react with HPO4 2- and PO4 3- ions to form dicalcium dihydrogen phosphate (DCPD), also called brushite, according to the reactions described in the Equations 6-9: Ca2++HPO42−+2H2O→CaHPO4·2H2ODCPD (6)

Other form of calcium-phosphates such as octacalcium phosphate (OCP), hydroxyapatite (HA) and tricalcium phosphate (TCP) could also form according to the following reactions: 4Ca2++HPO 42−+2PO43−+2.5H2O → Ca4HPO43· 2.5H2O OCP (7) 5Ca2++3PO43+OH−→ Ca5 PO43 OH HA (8) 3Ca2++2PO 43−→ Ca3PO42 TCP (9)

However, at the beginning of the precipitation process, DCPD formation prevails because of two major factors:Absence of sufficient OH− ions for generation of HA.DCPD is stable at pH < 5 and its precipitation is promoted in the presence of a low amount of OH− ions (acidic condition).

Final preparation of specimens
After electrodeposition, the coated Ti discs were washed with distilled water before entering a clean room for packaging in PA/PE double bags.

Gamma sterilization at 25 kGy was performed on the sealed packages (Group “Ti-AM + Bru”).

A second set of uncoated AM discs was also washed, packaged and gamma sterilized under the same conditions. This was used as a reference for in vitro testing (Group “Ti-AM”).

Chemical analysis by means of ICP
The coating has been analyzed by ICP-OES (inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry) in order to measure the content of elements and verify the absence of unwanted metals.

For this measurement, 25 cylindrical specimens (31 mm height, 12 mm diameter) were prepared under the same conditions as the specimens used for in-vitro testing. Unlike the other analyses, larger samples were used for ICP in order to ensure sufficient coating mass for the detection of trace elements, while ensuring that the deposition process remained identical.

Each specimen was weighted and then immersed into a beaker with 30 ml of distilled water and 1 ml of ultrapure nitric acid (Ultra-pure nitric acid 70%, Sigma Aldrich). Each specimen remained in this solution for 1 min, then put in an oven at 90 °C, for 90 min. After cooling at room temperature, the specimen was re-weighted. Five specimens were immersed in the nitric acid solution in order the increase the amount of diluted coating mass. The obtained solution was finally put into a graduated flask filled up the to 100 ml mark with distilled water.

The procedure was repeated five times in order to have five solutions.

The same procedure was applied also to five blank specimens, i.e. specimens made of the same substrate materials, but not coated with brushite.

Each solution was then measured three times with an ICP-OES Spectro CirOs CCD (SPECTRO Analytical Instruments GmbH, Germany) instrument.

Cell lines
Human MSCs (Lonza Technologies, Walkersville, MD United States) were cultured in mesenchymal stem cell growth medium (MSCGM™ Bullet Kit, Lonza, Walkersville, MD United States) to expand cells without inducing differentiation. The culture medium was changed every 3 days, and cells were split at 80%–90% of confluence using StemPro Accutase (Gibco by Life Technologies, Grand Islands, NY United States). To perform osteogenic differentiation, MSCs were treated with MSC mesenchymal stem cell osteogenic differentiation medium (OM) (hMSC Osteogenic Differentiation Bullet Kit™, Lonza) and to underlined the role of brushite coating on osteogenic differentiation, MSCs were also maintained in basal medium (BM) (hMSCs Basal Growth Medium Bullet KitTM, Lonza).

Establishment of a co-culture system of MSCs and Ti alloys
For transcriptome analysis, MSC cells were seeded (15x104 cells/well in MW 6 well) in OM and BM into 6-well plate (Costa, NY, United States); the day after, hMSC cells were co-cultured for 7 and 14 days, using a transwell system (Corning® Transwell®, 0.4 µm Pore Polycarbonate Membrane Insert), through indirect contact with the coated and uncoated titanium alloy samples (Ti-AM; Ti-AM + Bru), placed at the top of the well in the culture chamber. 500 μl of culture medium was added to each 1 g Ti alloy disc. As an internal experimental control, hMSCs were cultured alone in BM and OM. On 7 and 14 days, the complete medium was removed, hMSCs were washed twice with phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and then immediately processed for RNA extraction.

RNA extraction and real-time PCR
Total RNA was extracted using the commercially available TRIzol Reagent (ThermoFisher Scientific), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA was reverse transcripted to cDNA using the HighCapacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, Fisher Scientific Italia) and relative real-time PCR was performed in duplicates for each data point, using QuantiTect Primers (Qiagen).

Changes in the target mRNA content relative to the housekeeping gene β-actin were determined with the 2−ΔΔCT method (Livak and Schmittgen, 2001).

Transcriptomic analysis
Libraries were generated from 1 µg of RNA using the TruSeq mRNA V2 Prep Kit with Ribo-Zero Gold (Illumina, San Diego, CA, United States). The quality and yield of the prepared libraries were assessed using the Qubit 2.0 fluorometer (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, United States) for quantitative analysis and the TapeStation 4200 system (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, United States) for qualitative analysis. Sequencing of the libraries was performed on the NextSeq™ 550 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, United States) with 2 × 76 cycles. Quality control of the raw sequencing data was performed with FastQC (v0.11.9, Babraham Institute). Both low-quality read removal and adapter sequence trimming were performed with trimmomatic (v0.32) (Bolger et al., 2014). The remaining sequences from the cleaning step were mapped to the human reference genome hg19 with STAR (v2.7.0) (Dobin et al., 2013) and transcript amounts were measured with RSEM (v1.3.3) (Li and Dewey, 2011). Gene expression level was normalized by Transcripts Per Million (TPM). To identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), those transcripts whose fold change was between ≥1.5 and ≤0.6666 with a p-value <0.05 were accepted as DEGs. DEGs were analyzed by hierarchical clustering using a “Euclidean distance” distance measure with R functions (v4.1.2).

Standard RNA-seq sequencing quality metrics are provided in Supplementary Figure S3.

The RNA-seq datasets generated during this study have been deposited and are available in the NCBI SRA database with the accession number: PRJNA1506358. The hyperlink to the database is the following: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/1506358.

Functional enrichment analysis
For functional gene annotation, the obtained sequences were annotated by searching various databases, including Gene Ontology (GO) and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). These deregulated genes were subjected to GO and KEGG significant enrichment analyses to identify the biological functions and related metabolic pathways in which these genes are involved. In figures, we only reported the significant top 10 ranked terms.

Analysis of supernatant soluble factors
The level of soluble factors in the cell culture supernatants was analyzed by multiplex-bead immunoassay. Procollagen type I alpha1 (COL1A1), tumor necrosis factor (TNF) alpha, transforming growth factor (TGF)-β1, transforming growth factor (TGF) -β2 and fibronectin (FN) were simultaneously measured by commercially available bead-based sandwich immunoassay kits (Luminex performance Assay multiplex kits, R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, United States) according to the manufacturer’s protocols.

Samples or standards were incubated with antibody-coated fluorescent microparticles (50 µl) coated with antibodies specific for each molecule into a 96-well plate After a washing step, samples were incubated with biotinylated antibody cocktail (50 µl) for 1 hour, followed by incubation with fluorescent streptavidin for 30 min. The reaction of sandwich immune complexes on distinct microparticle sets were detected (with) by using the Bio-Plex Protein Array System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, United States). The Bio-Plex Manager software version 6.0 (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, United States) were used for data analyses. Standard curves were employed to quantify soluble factor concentrations by a five-parameter logistic (5 PL) curve-fit. Schematic illustrations, statistical charts and plots were created using BioRender (https://BioRender.com).

Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 9.0 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, United States). Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from three independent experiments, each performed in triplicate. For qRT-PCR analyses, results are expressed as fold induction (FOI) of Ti-Bru relative to Ti-AM. Differences between experimental groups were evaluated using two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons test. For soluble factor quantification, two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test was used to assess the effects of treatment (Ti-Bru vs. Ti-AM), treatment time, and their interaction. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 (*), p < 0.005 (**), and p < 0.0005 (). Graphical figures were created using BioRender.com.

Chemical analysis by means of ICP
According to the weight differences recorded before and after immersion in nitric acid, the mass amount of brushite coating dissolved for each specimen ranged between 25.7 mg and 37.3 mg.

Table 1 shows the results of the three ICP measurements for each of the five solutions.

On each solution the concentrations of As, Pb and Hg were also assessed (As: λ = 228.812 nm, Pb: λ = 220.353 nm, Hg: λ = 194.227 nm) but their intensities were below the respective detection limits (As: 0.003 mg/L, Pb: 0.014 mg/L, Hg: 0.02 mg/L).

No other elements were detected in the five solutions obtained from the coated specimens, i.e., their signals were below the detection limits of the instrument used for this quantification.

Finally, ICP measurements of blank samples did not reveal the presence of any of these elements, that is, their signals were below the detection limits of the instrument used for quantification.

Global transcriptomic profiling of MSCs cultured on brushite-coated titanium under osteogenic conditions
Global gene expression profiling by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) was performed on hMSCs cultured for 7 days on brushite-coated (Ti-AM + Bru) and uncoated titanium (Ti-AM) alloys under osteogenic conditions to characterize early transcriptional responses. Differential expression analysis identified 390 significantly modulated genes (p < 0.05, |logFC| ≥ 0.5), including 131 upregulated and 259 downregulated transcripts, while 16,789 genes were not significantly affected. The overall distribution of differentially expressed genes is shown in the volcano plot (Figures 2A). Hierarchical clustering analysis of significantly differentially expressed genes demonstrated a clear separation between Ti-AM + Bru and Ti-AM samples, with consistent clustering within each experimental group (Supplementary Figure 1). The heatmap revealed distinct gene expression patterns, with clusters of genes showing reciprocal regulation between the two conditions, indicating a condition-specific transcriptional response. To further refine this analysis, the top 100 most significantly deregulated genes were selected (Figures 2B). These genes clearly discriminated between Ti-AM + Bru (“case”) and Ti-AM (“control”) samples, confirming the strong impact of brushite surface modification on the transcriptional profile of MSCs. The complete dataset, including baseMean, log2 FoldChange, lfcSE, statistical values, and p-values, is provided in Supplementary File 1. As reported in Table 2, upregulated genes contribute to biological processes critical for implant integration, including osteogenesis, inflammation, immune response, energy metabolism, and cell adhesion.

Downregulated genes in MSC on Ti-AM + Bru surfaces vs. MSC on Ti-AM surfaces are consistent with early implant healing, reflecting a shift from inflammation toward tissue regeneration and bone formation. This profile indicates activation of osteogenic pathways and resolution of early stress and immune responses, promoting a stable environment for osseointegration. As shown in Table 3, these changes support the expected progression toward successful implant integration.

Pathway enrichment analysis of up- and downregulated genes in osteogenic culture conditions
To provide an integrated view of the transcriptional response, differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed on MSCs cultured under the experimental conditions (Figures 3, 4). Upregulated genes were significantly associated with pathways involved in osteogenic commitment, developmental signaling, and metabolic adaptation. Reactome analysis highlighted enrichment of PCP protein localization, Hedgehog pathway activation, AXIN degradation, and regulation of RUNX2, RUNX3, and PTEN, suggesting a coordinated activation of osteogenic and differentiation-related programs. Consistently, KEGG analysis revealed enrichment of complement and coagulation cascades, N-glycan biosynthesis, proteasome activity, and Hedgehog signaling, suggesting the concurrent involvement of immune modulation, protein turnover, and developmental pathways. GO enrichment further supported these findings, showing enrichment of oxidoreductase and phosphatase activities, lipid and protein metabolic processes, mitochondrial electron transport, and oxidative stress–related responses, reflecting early metabolic and functional adaptation to the biomaterial interface.

Conversely, downregulated genes showed enrichment of pathways associated with proliferative signaling, cytoskeletal regulation, immune activation, and cellular stress responses. Reactome analysis identified pathways related to AKT signaling, Rho GTPase cycles (RHOB, RHOF), mismatch repair, and telomere-related pathways, suggesting potential alterations in proliferative activity and cytoskeletal remodeling. KEGG analysis identified enrichment of ABC transporters, while GO terms highlighted decreased DNA exonuclease activity, chemokine receptor signaling, Hsp90 binding, cholesterol efflux, fatty acid transport, and cAMP-responsive processes. Collectively, these results are consistent with a coordinated transcriptional shift characterized by activation of osteogenic and metabolic programs and concomitant attenuation of inflammatory, stress-related, and proliferative pathways, consistent with the establishment of a stable, pro-osteointegrative cellular state at the biomaterial interface (Figures 5, 6).

Transcriptomic response under basal conditions
To evaluate material-driven effects independently of osteogenic induction, global transcriptomic profiling was performed by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on MSCs cultured for 7 days on Ti-AM + Bru and Ti-AM under basal conditions. Differential expression analysis identified 613 significantly modulated genes (p < 0.05, |log2FC| ≥ 0.5), of which 343 were upregulated and 270 downregulated in Ti-AM + Bru compared to Ti-AM, while 15,109 genes were not significantly affected.

The overall distribution of differentially expressed genes is illustrated in the volcano plot (Figure 7A), highlighting a robust transcriptional response driven by the biomaterial surface even in the absence of osteogenic stimulation. Hierarchical clustering of the top 100 most significantly differentially expressed genes revealed a clear separation between Ti-AM + Bru and Ti-AM samples (Figure 7B).

Samples clustered according to surface type, indicating high intra-group consistency. The heatmap showed two major gene clusters with reciprocal expression patterns, with genes upregulated in Ti-AM + Bru consistently downregulated in Ti-AM samples, and vice versa (Supplementary Figure 2). The complete dataset, including baseMean, log2FoldChange, lfcSE, statistical values, and p-values, is provided in Supplementary File 2. RNA-seq analysis revealed a broad transcriptional reprogramming in MSCs cultured on brushite-coated titanium under basal conditions, involving genes linked to extracellular matrix remodeling, chemokine signaling, cell cycle regulation, and intracellular trafficking (Table 4). Upregulation of MMP1, MMP3, CXCL1, CXCL5, and CXCL6 was consistent with increased matrix turnover and chemokine activity, reflecting an active cell–material interface. Concurrently, increased expression of DNA damage response and cell cycle regulators (BUB1, CHEK2, RAD17, FANCM) suggests a controlled proliferative state, supported by metabolic and redox gene activation (TXN, ERO1L, HIGD1A), reflecting early bioenergetic adaptation to the biomaterial surface.

In addition, Ti-AM + Bru surfaces induce an early shift toward a quiescent, pro-regenerative MSC state characterized by coordinated modulation of contractile, fibrotic, mechanotransductive, and stress-responsive programs, with reduced ECM stiffening, adhesion strength, and inflammatory signaling (Table 5).

Pathway enrichment analysis of up- and downregulated genes in basal culture conditions
To provide an integrated view of the transcriptional response, differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed on MSCs cultured under the experimental conditions (Figures 8–11). Integrated pathway analysis indicates an early metabolic and translational activation accompanied by modulation of immune-inflammatory signaling and reduced mechanosensitive adhesion pathways, consistent with a material-driven shift toward a pro-regenerative MSC state (Figures 8–11). In addition, a set of 25 genes was consistently modulated in MSCs cultured on brushite-coated titanium alloy compared to uncoated titanium, both under basal and osteogenic conditions. Most genes showed concordant regulation across conditions, indicating a robust and material-driven transcriptional response. Downregulated Genes: Primarily involved in ECM organization, cytoskeletal dynamics, and intracellular signaling. Downregulation occurred in both osteogenic and basal conditions, suggesting reduced activity in these pathways. Upregulated Genes: Related to metabolism, immunomodulation, and cell survival, with upregulation observed across both conditions, suggesting enhanced metabolic and survival pathways. A small subset of genes (e.g., ABCA7, SPTBN2) exhibited opposite regulation depending on the culture condition, suggesting a context-dependent response (Table 6).

Brushite incorporation was associated with a stable transcriptional signature in MSCs, potentially priming them for osteointegration by modulating key metabolic, immune, and cytoskeletal pathways.

Validation of osteogenic markers at transcriptional and protein levels
The expression of selected osteogenesis-related genes was assessed in MSCs cultured for 7 days under osteogenic conditions on Ti-AM + Bru and Ti-AM substrates. Quantitative gene expression analysis also confirmed the RNA-seq results, showing increased expression of key osteogenic regulators, including RUNX2, BMP2, and SMAD family members, in hMSCs cultured on brushite-coated titanium compared with uncoated titanium (Figure 12).

Protein-level validation of the early pro-osteogenic response
Importantly, these transcriptomic findings were further supported by protein-level validation using Bio-Plex multiplex assays. In MSCs cultured on brushite-functionalized titanium alloy under both basal and osteogenic conditions for 7 and 14 days of cultured, a significant upregulation, compared to Ti-AM, of TNFα, procollagen type I alpha 1 (COL1A1), fibronectin (FN), TGF-β1 and TGF-β2 was observed at early time point in both conditions. This effect was particularly pronounced under 7days compared to 14days culture conditions, highlighting the synergistic interaction between surface chemistry and differentiation cues. The early increase in COL1A1 and fibronectin supports rapid extracellular matrix deposition and organization at the biomaterial interface, while the upregulation of TGF-β1 and TGFB-β2 confirms activation of key osteogenic and remodelling pathways (Linsley et al., 2013; Schierano et al., 2021). Interestingly, the increase in COL1A1 protein levels at 7 days occurred despite a transcriptional stabilization or reduction of certain collagen subunits (e.g., COL1A2), suggesting a complex post-transcriptional regulation during early matrix deposition (Pan et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2019). At the same time, TNFα upregulation suggests a tightly regulated early inflammatory response that contributes to cell recruitment and signalling cross-talk required for successful osteointegration (Figure 13). These protein-level data provide critical validation of the transcriptomic results and, importantly, demonstrate that brushite promotes an early upregulation of osteointegrative signalling pathways, rather than merely affecting late-stage differentiation marker (Raimondi et al., 2025; Shaik et al., 2019; Ivanovski et al., 2011). The fact that these effects are already evident at 7 days underscores the role of brushite as an active bifunctional coating capable of accelerating the initial phases of cell commitment and matrix formation.

Discussion
Brushite-coated Ti6Al4V alloys enhance osteogenic activity and biomineralization while modulating the MSC secretome to promote factors critical for bone healing, highlighting their significant potential to improve the biological performance and long-term success of orthopedic prosthetic implants (Raimondi et al., 2025). In vitro studies most often assess these effects at later time points (14–21 days) when osteogenic differentiation and matrix mineralization are more pronounced. These late-stage analyses are particularly informative, as they capture the peak of osteogenic activity and provide a comprehensive picture of how brushite coatings influence bone regeneration. However, early-time analyses are equally important, as they reveal initial cellular responses such as adhesion, proliferation, and early signaling events that ultimately set the stage for subsequent differentiation and mineralization (Zhang et al., 2021; Van De Peppel et al., 2017). In addition to the canonical osteogenic culture conditions, studying MSC on brushite-coated titanium under basal conditions can provide valuable insights into the material’s intrinsic ability to modulate cellular behavior. Such analyses allow the assessment of early cellular responses, secretome changes, and potential osteoinductive effects that are independent of exogenous osteogenic stimuli, providing insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying bone regeneration in physiological settings. Building on our previous study demonstrating that brushite-coated Ti6Al4V alloys enhance osteogenic activity and modulate the mesenchymal stem cell secretome, in the present study we focused on the early cellular response to the material. Using NGS analysis, we examined MSCs at 7 days in response to brushite-coated versus uncoated titanium under both osteogenic and basal conditions. We chose the transwell configuration intentionally in order to reproduce the early peri-implant microenvironment, in which recruited MSCs initially respond to diffusible biochemical signals released by the biomaterial before establishing direct contact with the implant surface. This design allowed us to assess the intrinsic effects of the coating (“priming”) on MSC molecular pathways, providing insights into the initial mechanisms that may shape subsequent osteogenic differentiation and bone regeneration. As previously characterized, brushite coatings on Ti6Al4V substrates fabricated via laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) exhibited the expected brushite phase, characteristic cauliflower-like morphology by SEM, a Ca/P ratio consistent with stoichiometric brushite, rapid dissolution in acidic conditions, adequate adhesion, and an average thickness of ∼27 μm (Raimondi et al., 2025). In particular, the reported dissolution tests conducted according to ASTM F1926 standards demonstrate that the brushite coating almost completely dissolves within 2 hours in HEPES buffer at pH 7.4. Under more acidic conditions (MES buffer, pH 5.5), which can simulate the initial inflammatory microenvironment post-implantation, this rate increases significantly. In the present study, ICP-OES analysis confirmed that Ca and P are the main elements constituting the coating as expected. No elements are present in a concentration higher than the limits indicated by ASTM1609 (F04 Committee, 2026). Trace elements like Fe, Cu, Zn are often found in calcium-phosphates, and the measured concentrations are therefore considered to be acceptable: unsubstituted apatites do not exists in biological systems (Dorozhkin, 2009) and ion substitution impurities are present also in natural bone (Eliaz and Metoki, 2017). Moreover, the bioactivity of calcium phosphate coating can be improved by the presence of such ionic substitutions with different positive effects (Drevet et al., 2023). On each solution toxic elements as, Pb and Hg were not found. For all the cases, concentration for these elements was below the limits imposed by ISO 13779-2 (ISO13779-2:2018: Technical committee: ISO/TC 150/SC 1, 2024) and ASTM F1609 standards (F04 Committee, 2026). All these analytical results provide evidence that the transcriptomic signatures observed in the current study are specifically driven by the bioactive ionic environment generated by the brushite dissolution, primarily the release of calcium and phosphate ions, ensuring that the observed cellular responses were not confounded by impurities. With the material properties established, attention was subsequently directed toward understanding how these features translate into biological functionality. Brushite-coated titanium surfaces elicited a robust and coherent transcriptional response in MSCs under both basal and osteogenic conditions, demonstrating that surface-mediated cues act independently of soluble differentiation factors and are further enhanced in an osteogenic milieu. As first stated, this response was investigated at an early time point, a phase that is often underexplored in favor of later differentiation stages, but which was specifically selected to capture the initial cell–material interaction dynamics preceding stable lineage commitment. This early window of analysis allowed the identification of primary transcriptional adaptations driven directly by surface properties rather than downstream differentiation events, providing mechanistic insight into the earliest phases of MSC reprogramming at the biomaterial interface. The study reveals that brushite-coated titanium surfaces induce a distinct early transcriptional response in MSCs under osteogenic conditions. Transcriptomic profiling by bulk RNA-seq revealed widespread transcriptional remodeling at day 7, as evidenced by the large number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified, with a predominant downregulation, indicating that brushite modification selectively reprograms transcription rather than broadly activating gene expression. Hierarchical clustering and heatmap analyses showed a clear segregation between brushite-coated and uncoated titanium, highlighting a robust material-dependent effect on MSC behavior. Among the upregulated genes, BMP2, FZD3, and SMURF2 are particularly noteworthy, as they are central components of the BMP and Wnt signaling pathways that drive osteoblast differentiation (Zhang et al., 2013; Marcellini et al., 2012). Their early upregulation at 7 days suggests that brushite-coated titanium can prime MSCs, activating key molecular pathways that initiate osteogenic commitment and potentially facilitate subsequent bone integration. Reactome and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses further highlighted the involvement of RUNX2 regulation and Hedgehog signaling, both of which are well-established early drivers of osteoblast differentiation. In agreement with other findings demonstrating the role of SLC20A1-mediated phosphate uptake in ATP-dependent osteogenic signaling (Shih et al., 2014), the observed upregulation of SLC20A1 suggests enhanced commitment toward matrix mineralization, indicating that MSC are primed for matrix deposition and biomineralization. These findings are consistent with previous reports demonstrating that early activation of RUNX2 and Hedgehog pathways, together with enhanced phosphate handling, orchestrates the initiation of osteogenic programs in response to biomaterials (Wang et al., 2025; Komori, 2025). The osteogenic program is characterized by enhanced mitochondrial function and elevated oxygen consumption, reflecting a preferential reliance on oxidative phosphorylation over glycolysis. This metabolic transition provides the energetic support necessary for matrix deposition and mineralization (Smith and Eliseev, 2021). The transcriptional profile revealed increased expression of metabolic genes such as NDUFA9 and MTHFD2L, suggesting a shift toward elevated mitochondrial activity, which is essential to support osteogenic differentiation and matrix production. Concurrently, the upregulation of immune-related genes including IL8, OAS1, and IFIT1 is compatible with a controlled inflammatory response, consistent with reports that early, modulated inflammation is necessary to orchestrate bone healing and facilitate implant integration (Jalloob and HandoolAlfattli, 2025). Together, these findings align with the concept that brushite-coated titanium not only primes MSCs for osteogenesis but also coordinates metabolic and immune pathways critical for successful early-stage bone regeneration. Validation by qRT-PCR at 7 days under osteogenic conditions confirmed the upregulation of key osteogenic regulators, including RUNX2, BMP2, SMAD1, and SMAD4, corroborating the transcriptomic evidence of an early osteogenic priming effect exerted by brushite-coated titanium surfaces. Although NOTCH4, WNT7B, and BMP8B were downregulated, this finding should not be interpreted as an overall inhibition of the corresponding signaling pathways. Instead, changes in the expression of individual ligands may represent a temporal regulatory mechanism accompanying pathway activation. Notably, despite the early downregulation of BMP8B, the higher expression of BMP2 and SMAD signaling components, together with the enrichment of the BMP pathway, implies a significant osteogenic response during the early phases of osseointegration.

In particular, the reduction of NOTCH4 aligns with reports that reduced Notch signaling facilitates the exit from a progenitor-like state and supports osteoblast maturation (Engin et al., 2008); notably, in vitro studies have demonstrated that Notch signaling can exert both stimulatory and inhibitory effects on stromal cell osteoblastic differentiation, depending on factors such as cell type, differentiation stage, and the timing of pathway activation (Luo et al., 2019). The observed suppression of AKT signaling, Rho GTPase activity, and DNA mismatch repair pathways indicates reduced proliferative and stress responses (Tanaka et al., 2018; Meyers et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2024), while concomitant downregulation of immune-related genes (SAA2, ICAM5) suggests attenuation of early inflammatory signaling, collectively consistent with stabilization of a differentiated state (Thomas and Jaganathan, 2022; Xu et al., 2023). Taken together, these findings support a model where brushite-coated titanium surfaces promote, in osteogenic condition, an early transition from a reactive, proliferation-associated phenotype to a more metabolically active and differentiation-oriented state. This transition, marked by the activation of osteogenic signaling and immune modulation, is crucial for early osseointegration. Importantly, these effects occur at an early time point (7 days), emphasizing the role of surface chemistry in directing MSC fate before the full activation of mature osteogenic markers.

Under basal conditions, brushite-coated titanium surfaces also induced a distinct transcriptional response in MSCs, independent of osteogenic stimulation. RNA-seq analysis revealed a broad transcriptional reprogramming, marked by the upregulation of genes associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, chemokine signaling, and intracellular trafficking. The upregulation of MMP1, MMP3, CXCL1, CXCL5, and CXCL6 suggests potential increased matrix turnover and chemokine-mediated signaling, reflecting an active cell-material interface. Indeed, biomaterials that induce upregulation of specific MMPs and CXCLs can effectively promote MSC-mediated bone regeneration by optimizing the local environment for both mineralization and vascularization (Shaik et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025; Khoswanto, 2023). Enrichment of genes involved in cell cycle regulation and DNA damage response (BUB1, CHEK2, RAD17) suggests a highly proliferative yet tightly regulated cellular state (Shaikh et al., 2023). These genes play essential roles in preserving genomic integrity during the rapid expansion and subsequent differentiation of MSCs into osteoblasts. The increased expression of metabolic and redox-related genes (e.g., TXN, ERO1L, HIGD1A) suggests an early bioenergetic adaptation, supported by enrichment of mitochondrial pathways. Pathway enrichment also highlighted a dominant signature of translational activation, with strong enrichment of ribosomal activity and macromolecule biosynthesis, indicating increased biosynthetic capacity (Lee et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017). In parallel, multiple datasets revealed activation of stress-response and regulatory pathways, including ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, SUMOylation, and DNA repair mechanisms, suggesting tight control of protein turnover and genomic stability. Furthermore, the activation of inflammatory pathways, such as IL-17 and TNF signaling, points to early and critical mediator in immunomodulatory processes (Sjakste and Riekstiņa, 2021; Pan et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Park et al., 2024; Hess et al., 2009). Downregulated genes may be associated with attenuation of focal adhesion, integrin signaling, and actin cytoskeleton organization. The attenuation of Rho GTPase signaling suggests reduced cytoskeletal dynamics and mechanotransduction, further supported by decreased enrichment of EPH-ephrin signaling and intercellular communication pathways. Taken together, these findings support the hypothesis that brushite coating induces a transcriptional shift in basal conditions characterized by enhanced metabolic, translational, and biosynthetic activity, coupled with suppressed adhesion and cytoskeletal signaling networks. Moreover, even at baseline, the material seems to elicit a biologically active interface rather than a passive cellular state. Our results reveal a sophisticated, context-dependent regulation of MSC cell-cycle dynamics. Under basal conditions, the brushite surface seems to promote a controlled proliferative state (marked by BUB1 and CHEK2 upregulation), likely facilitating initial colonization of the 3D-printed scaffold. Conversely, upon exposure to osteogenic cues, we observed a coordinated reduction of proliferative pathways (including AKT signaling and Rho GTPases), indicating a interesting shift toward terminal differentiation. This material-driven priming effect appears to predispose the cells for rapid extracellular matrix deposition, as further evidenced by increased COL1A1 and TGF-β1/2 secretion at the protein level, even prior to the onset of late-stage mineralization markers (Pan et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2019). Comparison between osteogenic and basal conditions revealed a consistent set of 25 genes modulated across both environments, representing a material-dependent transcriptional signature independent of differentiation cues. This set includes downregulated genes related to ECM organization and cytoskeletal dynamics, and upregulated genes involved in metabolism, immunomodulation, and cell survival (e.g., NT5E, PDCD10, PLA2G4A, SLC16A6). A small subset of genes displayed condition-dependent regulation, reflecting a context-specific response to the surface modification. Overall, these results suggest that brushite-coated titanium surfaces may induce an early adaptive state in MSCs, characterized by increased metabolic and biosynthetic activity, controlled inflammatory signaling, and reduced mechanotransduction. This transcriptional signature appears to prime the cells for subsequent osteogenic commitment under inductive conditions, positioning brushite as a promising material for enhancing the early stages of osseointegration and improving titanium-based implant performance. The transcriptional profile observed at 7 days suggests that brushite-coated titanium-alloy surfaces do not yet induce complete osteogenic differentiation, but rather promote an early cellular state that predisposes MSCs toward subsequent osteogenic commitment. The combination of enhanced metabolic and biosynthetic activity, controlled inflammatory signaling, and reduced mechanotransduction may define an early priming state preceding overt osteogenic differentiation. Since most studies primarily investigate late-stage osteogenesis and mineralization, this early adaptive transcriptional program has likely remained underexplored. These transcriptomic findings were further supported by Bio-Plex multiplex analysis, confirming that the early transcriptional program induced by brushite-coated titanium surfaces is translated into a functional protein output (Hamed et al., 2023; Wall et al., 2009). MSCs cultured on brushite-functionalized titanium showed increased secretion of extracellular matrix components (COL1A1 and FN1), osteogenic and tissue-remodeling factors (TGF-β1 and TGF-β2), and a moderate increase in TNF-α under both basal and osteogenic conditions (Linsley et al., 2013).

The enhanced production of matrix-related proteins supports the establishment of a structurally competent extracellular environment favorable early osteointegration, while the upregulation of TGF-β signaling further suggests activation of pathways involved in MSC commitment and matrix maturation (Barradas et al., 2013). In parallel, the moderate increase in TNF-α is consistent with a controlled pro-inflammatory response known to contribute to the early stages of bone healing and implant integration (Lee et al., 2021; Ince et al., 2008; Huo and Yue, 2020). Importantly, these effects were observed even in the absence of exogenous osteogenic stimuli, indicating that brushite exerts an intrinsic bioactive effect on MSC behavior. Overall, the Bio-Plex data reinforce the transcriptomic evidence, supporting the hypothesis that brushite-coated titanium surfaces promote a primary adaptive and pro-osteogenic cellular state that may facilitate subsequent osteointegration. Overall, the present study highlights the importance of early transcriptomic adaptations in defining biomaterial-driven osteogenic commitment and identifies brushite coatings as promising modulators of the initial phases of bone–implant integration.

Conclusion
In conclusion, this study identifies brushite-coated Ti6Al4V as a highly active bio-interface capable of modulating early MSC transcriptional programs well before overt differentiation occurs. Our findings highlight a critical 7-day regulatory window where the coating triggers a robust ‘priming’ state characterized by enrichment of genes related to pro-osteogenic signaling (BMP, Wnt, Hedgehog), metabolic/mitochondrial reprogramming, and a controlled immunomodulatory response Notably, the identification of a stable 25-gene core signature across both basal and osteogenic conditions demonstrates that brushite possesses intrinsic bioactivity independent of soluble biochemical cues. These transcriptomic insights, validated by functional protein secretion data, confirm that brushite does not act as a passive scaffold but as a dynamic driver of cell behavior. These findings emphasize the importance of early molecular events in biomaterial-driven osseointegration and provide strong support for the clinical application of brushite-functionalized surfaces in high-performance orthopedic and dental implants.

paper.title: Functional Roles of Wnt/β-catenin Pathway Components in Pre-Basal Cell Carcinoma-like Cell Proliferation and Survival.
paper.abstract: Wnt/β-catenin signaling supports basal cell carcinoma (BCC)-like tumor initiation in mice. However, nuclear β-catenin is frequently detected in well-developed BCCs and correlates with increased tumor cell proliferation, suggesting that Wnt/β-catenin signaling may also promote BCC development. Our analysis of published single-cell transcriptomic datasets from human BCCs revealed that multiple Wnt pathway components, including Wntless (WLS) and the Wnt receptor Frizzled2 (FZD2), are enriched in specific BCC cell populations with active Hedgehog (Hh) signaling. Using an inducible mouse model with forced epithelial expression of the Hh activator GLI2ΔN, we found that Wnt-responsive Axin2+ epidermal basal cells contribute to BCC-like tumor formation. Deletion of epithelial β-catenin or WLS several days after GLI2ΔN expression significantly reduced tumor cell proliferation without affecting BCC marker expression, Hh pathway activity, or apoptosis. These findings indicate that Wnt/β-catenin signaling acts downstream of Hh signaling to promote pre-BCC-like cell proliferation. Furthermore, Wnt receptor Fzd2 depletion reduced tumor cell proliferation and induced apoptosis, suggesting that FZD2 promotes proliferation and survival through β-catenin-dependent and -independent mechanisms. These findings identify Wnt pathway components as key regulators of pre-BCC-like cell proliferation and survival.

paper.title: Mesenchymal Stromal Cells Fuel Immunometabolic Reprogramming of Type 2 Conventional Dendritic Cells to Alleviate Systemic Sclerosis.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the clinical efficacy and underlying mechanisms of mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) therapy in systemic sclerosis (SSc).

METHODS: We prospectively evaluated the efficacy of MSC therapy in SSc patients. To elucidate the therapeutic mechanisms, we integrated paired multi-omics data: proteomics (n=7), metabolomics (n=7), and both bulk (n=6) and single-cell (n=2) RNA-seq. Baseline disease-associated signatures were mainly defined by publicly available datasets of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs, 21 SSc vs. 6 healthy donors).

RESULTS: MSC therapy significantly ameliorated skin fibrosis (median mRSS decrease 7.0 [IQR, 3.8-9.3], P < 0.05) and stabilized lung function after 6 months. In parallel with these clinical improvements, plasma proteomic analysis demonstrated that MSC therapy suppressed Hedgehog-mediated fibrotic pathways (Padj < 0.05). Transcriptomic profiling revealed that pathogenic type 2 conventional dendritic cells (cDC2s) exhibit intrinsic oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) defects (Padj < 0.05) in SSc. MSC therapy effectively repaired these defects and concurrently suppressed cDC2-related inflammatory pathways in PBMCs and plasma (Padj < 0.05). Consistent with these findings, single-cell RNA-seq revealed OXPHOS recovery in cDC2s alongside an increased proportion of homeostatic subsets.

CONCLUSIONS: Our study underscores the MSC-mediated immunometabolic reprogramming to restore immune homeostasis by targeting upstream OXPHOS defects of cDC2s in SSc.

paper.title: Phospholipid phosphatase 2 drives liver repair and regeneration after acute liver injury.
paper.abstract: Acute liver injury is commonly caused by overdose-drug, toxins, or ischemia. The liver possesses a remarkable regenerative capacity, wherein metabolic remodeling plays a crucial role in restoring hepatic function and homeostasis. However, the specific metabolic shift that initiates hepatocyte regeneration remains unclear. Here, we employed multi-time-point multi-omics analyses to demonstrate that phosphatidylethanolamine undergoes a dynamic metabolic reprogramming, with phospholipid phosphatase 2 (PLPP2) exhibiting synchronous changes among the enzymes regulating PE metabolism. Liver biopsy samples from patients with drug-induced liver injury corroborated the PLPP2 alterations. In murine models, hepatocyte-specific deletion of PLPP2 exacerbated acute liver injury. Mechanistically, the resolution of ER stress was accompanied by a robust upregulation of PLPP2 during the regenerative phase. This shift promotes liver repair and regeneration by initiating the PE biosynthesis. PE, upon binding to PEBP1, modulated its affinity and strengthened its interaction with GLI1, thereby disrupting the association between lTCH and GLI1 and preventing the ubiquitination and degradation of GLI1. Additionally, PE promotes autophagy by facilitating the lipidation of LC3B. The increase in ER-localized PE mediated by PLPP2 also contributed to the alleviation of ER stress, thus establishing a positive feedback loop. Pharmacologic activation of PLPP2 or supplementation with ethanolamine may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for acute liver injury.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Acute liver injury (ALI) is a clinically significant condition characterized by the rapid onset of hepatocellular damage, leading to impaired liver function within days or weeks. It is typically triggered by factors such as drug toxicity (most notably acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, which is the leading cause of drug-induced liver injury (DILI)) as well as viral hepatitis, ischemia, or autoimmune responses.1 ALI is associated with elevated transaminase levels, coagulopathy, and, in severe cases, acute liver failure (ALF).1 Given its role as a leading cause of hepatic emergencies and high mortality in fulminant cases, studying ALI is a critical clinical imperative. The rapid progression from hepatocyte necrosis to systemic inflammatory response syndrome and multi-organ dysfunction syndrome creates a narrow therapeutic window. Current management remains largely supportive, lacking specific agents to halt the cycle of regulated cell death. Therefore, focused research is essential to develop targeted therapies. This will enable the discovery of early biomarkers and effective treatments, reducing reliance on liver transplantation and improving survival.

ALI exhibits a biphasic progression, characterized by an initial phase of innate immune activation and hepatocyte damage, followed by a repair phase marked by inflammation resolution and hepatocyte regeneration.2–4 Previous studies have demonstrated that metabolic reprogramming serves as a critical adaptive mechanism for mitigating ALI. Pericentral hepatocytes upregulate asparagine synthetase expression, converting glutamine to asparagine to aid hepatoprotection.5 Additionally, elevated Mas receptor activity in hepatocytes promotes lipophagy and fatty acid oxidation via the AKT-FOXO1 pathway, alleviating APAP-induced acute liver injury (AILI).6 These findings underscore how tailored metabolic adaptations act as endogenous protective strategies. However, the precise metabolic shift driving liver regeneration after ALI remains poorly defined. Identifying these key mechanisms may provide novel therapeutic targets for enhancing liver recovery.

Emerging evidence from multiple organ systems has increasingly underscored the critical role of phospholipid metabolism in orchestrating tissue regeneration. Specifically, a growing body of research has established that sphingolipid metabolism is indispensable for cardiac regeneration in mammals, as it modulates key proliferative and survival signals in cardiomyocytes.7 In parallel, the regulation of glycerolipid metabolism within neurons has been shown to critically dictate the extent and success of axonal regrowth and functional recovery following central nervous system injury.8 Consistent with these cross-tissue observations, recent preclinical work has revealed that either exogenous phosphatidic acid (PA) administration or pharmacological activation of the anabolic cardiolipin synthesis pathway attenuates ALl and enhances hepatocyte regeneration in mice.9 Collectively, these data point toward a compelling concept: the dynamic regulation of phospholipid metabolism may constitute a phylogenetically conserved, fundamental mechanism that governs the efficiency of tissue repair and regeneration across a wide spectrum of biological contexts.

Phospholipids, encompassing major classes such as phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and other related lipid species, are not only fundamental structural constituents of cellular membranes but also serve as critical mediators of membrane dynamics, intracellular signaling transduction, and overall cellular metabolism.10 Although previous studies have firmly established that PE and its associated autophagy play important roles in the contexts of aging and cancer,11,12 the specific contribution and functional significance of PE in the pathophysiology of ALI remain remarkably underexplored and poorly defined. In this study, we employed multi-timepoint multi-omics approaches to, for the first time, systematically delineate and demonstrate that PE metabolism is indispensable for hepatic repair and regeneration following ALI. Further investigations identified phospholipid phosphatase 2 (PLPP2) as a key metabolic enzyme mediating PE biosynthesis in the context of ALI and regulating hepatic repair and regeneration. Functional studies demonstrated that PE synthesized by PLPP2 not only promoted liver repair via the well-characterized autophagy pathway but also prevented the ubiquitination of GLI1 via altering the affinity of PE binding protein 1 (PEBP1), thereby regulating hepatocyte regeneration. Taken together, these integrated findings definitively establish PLPP2 as a promising and previously unrecognized therapeutic target for accelerating recovery from ALI.

Multi-timepoint and multi-omics analyses uncover dynamic remodeling of phospholipid metabolism following AILI
To investigate the dynamic changes in ALI and elucidate the molecular mechanisms governing hepatocyte regeneration, we performed proteomic analysis of liver tissues and hepatic enzyme assay of peripheral blood collected at multiple time points post-APAP treatment (Fig. 1a, b and Supplementary Fig. 1a, c). Unsupervised clustering analysis of the proteomic data revealed distinct temporal patterns, with high similarity observed between the 0 h and 168 h time points (representing pre- and post-injury baselines), the 6 h and 24 h time points (acute injury phase), and the 48 h, 72 h, and 96 h time points (recovery phase) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Further classification of all differentially expressed proteins into eight distinct clusters based on their temporal expression trajectories identified unique protein expression patterns in the entire process (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Heatmaps revealed significant upregulation of proteins involved in the apoptotic, necrotic, and inflammatory pathways within 48 h post-APAP (Fig. 1c). These findings were corroborated by histopathological evidence of hepatocellular death and inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 1d), as well as elevated serum ALT and AST levels (Fig. 1b). It supports the hypothesis that the injury phase predominantly occurs within the first 48 h post-APAP.Fig. 1Multi-timepoint and multi-omics analyses uncover dynamic remodeling of phospholipid metabolism following AILI. a Schematic diagram of liver tissues collection from mice at seven time points following AILI. Proteomics and metabolomics were integrated to delineate the entire temporal progression-from injury to repair. b Serum ALT and AST levels assayed by ELISA at indicated time points post APAP (n = 6, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). c Heat maps show expression of members of apoptosis, necrosis and inflammation pathways (n = 3, proteomics). d Representative gross liver photographs and intrahepatic staining with quantification of H&E (necrotic areas circled with white lines), TUNEL (apoptosis) (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). e Heat map shows expression of the cell proliferation pathway (n = 3, proteomics). f Immunohistochemical staining with quantification of mouse liver tissues for Ki67 and PCNA (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, **p < 0.01; ****p < 0.0001). g Representative FCM plots and quantification of MoMFs, KCs, and neutrophils in mouse liver tissues at indicated time points post APAP (n = 3, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). h The changes of APAP-related metabolites in metabolomics (n = 6, metabolomics). i The intersection of enriched pathways from multi-omics analysis for three couples, including 48 h vs 6 h, 72 h vs 6 h, and 96 h vs 6 h. j The pathways co-enriched by proteomics and metabolomics at 48 h and 6 h after APAP

The liver entered the repair phase at 48 h post-APAP. During this stage, the expression of proteins associated with cell proliferation was markedly upregulated (Fig. 1e), as further corroborated by immunohistochemical staining for the proliferative markers Ki67 and PCNA (Fig. 1f). Consistently, both KEGG pathway analysis and GSEA demonstrated significant enrichment and upregulation of cell proliferation-related pathways at 48 h post-APAP (Supplementary Fig. 1e–g).

To comprehensively characterize the dynamic inflammatory response throughout the course of ALI, we performed liver perfusions at seven time points and analyzed non-parenchymal cells via flow cytometry (FCM). Kupffer cells sharply decreased during liver injury but recovered to baseline after repair completion. In contrast, neutrophils and infiltrating macrophages (iMФs) surged during injury and declined during repair. Notably, Ly6Chigh iMФs gradually shifted to Ly6Clow iMФs as the liver transitioned from injury to repair3,13 (Fig. 1g). The transition from a pro-inflammatory to an anti-inflammatory microenvironment paralleled the aforementioned hepatocellular regeneration.

These results collectively indicate that 48 h post-APAP constitutes a critical temporal window during which the liver undergoes a phenotypic transition from injury to regeneration.

To investigate metabolic alterations following ALI, we also conducted an untargeted metabolomic profiling analysis using liver tissues collected from mice euthanized at seven time points post-APAP (Supplementary Fig. 1h, j). Consistent with the findings shown in Fig. 1, the metabonomic heatmaps at 0, 72, 96, and 168 h exhibited high similarity, whereas those at 6, 24, and 48 h demonstrated moderate similarity (Supplementary Fig. 1h). Based on the temporal dynamics of these differential metabolites, they were systematically grouped into eight distinct metabolic subtypes, thereby identifying characteristic metabolic transition patterns during the entire process (Supplementary Fig. 1i). Furthermore, hepatic APAP concentration peaked at 6 h post-APAP and subsequently declined gradually. Conversely, the glutathione (GSH) levels exhibited an inverse temporal pattern (Fig. 1h). To identify the key metabolic remodeling pathway driving liver regeneration, we performed an integrated proteomic and metabolomic analysis. Given that 6 h and 24 h time points represented the injury phase, while 48,72, and 96 h correspond to the repair phase, we analyzed the overlapping enriched pathways between not only H48 vs. H6, H72 vs. H6 and H96 vs. H6 but also H48 vs. H24, H72 vs. H24 and H96 vs. H24 (Fig. 1i and Supplementary Fig. 1k). The results demonstrated that the autophagy pathway was significantly enriched for the metabolite PE during the repair phase (Fig. 1j and Supplementary Fig. 1l). Previous studies have demonstrated that PE constitutes the predominant phospholipid component of autophagosome membranes, where it covalently conjugates with LC3 protein to form LC3-II (PE-LC3 complex), thereby facilitating autophagosome membrane elongation and closure.14 Therefore, we hypothesize that autophagy-associated metabolite PE exerts critical regulatory functions during the regenerative process.

PE exerts a protective effect against ALI
Initially, we assessed the temporal dynamics of autophagy. XBP1 transcriptionally regulates the expression of PLPP2 in ALI
To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying PLPP2 upregulation, we first investigated transcriptional regulation. Using the JASPAR and KnockTF databases, and based on sequence motif analysis and known regulatory relationships in the databases, we identified six potential transcription factors that may regulate the expression of PLPP2 (Fig. 3l). Among these, X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) was reported to be significantly upregulated in ALI, a finding consistent with our immunofluorescence data (Supplementary Fig. 3g). Moreover, hepatocyte-specific deletion of XBP1 attenuated ALI.18,19 Our previous studies on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) demonstrated that hepatic XBP1 expression is markedly upregulated and accelerates the progression of chronic inflammation through its regulatory role in lipid metabolism.20 Based on these findings, we hypothesize that XBP1 may transcriptionally suppress PLPP2 expression, thereby influencing PE metabolism. This hypothesis was validated by Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag), which showed that XBP1 bound to the PLPP2 promoter at 6 h post-APAP, while binding decreased at 48 h post-APAP (Fig. 3m). Subsequently, the online tool JASPAR was used to predict potential XBP1 binding sites (BS) in the PLPP2 promoter, revealing three putative binding sites (Fig. 3n and Supplementary Fig. 3h). Dual-luciferase reporter assays and ChlP assays demonstrated that BS1 is essential for the transcriptional inhibition of PLPP2 by XBP1, which was also verified by the immunofluorescence staining of HepG2 cells (Fig. 3o–q and Supplementary Fig. 3i). Further investigation revealed that both PLPP2 protein level and hepatic PE content were significantly elevated in Xbp1ΔHep mice, which promoted liver repair (Supplementary Fig. 3j–l). Thus, we infer that XBP1 modulates PLPP2 expression in ALI, thereby regulating PE biosynthesis.

PLPP2 acts as a pivotal regulatory hub integrating endoplasmic reticulum stress and phospholipid metabolism
To further validate the functional role of PLPP2 in ALI, we generated hepatocyte-specific Plpp2 knockout mice (Plpp2ΔHep) and hepatocyte-specific Plpp2 overexpression mice (AAV-Plpp2) (Supplementary Fig. 9a–e). Literature reports that the phospholipid composition within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) modulates ER stress through the regulation of unfolded protein.21 Interestingly, ER stress was significantly upregulated following Plpp2 knockout according to transcriptomic data (Supplementary Fig. 4a–c). We hypothesized that Plpp2 deficiency led to reduced ER PE levels, thereby inducing ER stress. The expression of ER stress-related genes at both the mRNA and protein levels supported the induction of ER stress by Plpp2 deficiency in AILI, while supplementation with Etn alleviated ER stress. Immunofluorescence staining results were consistent with these findings (Supplementary Fig. 4d–h). Furthermore, supplementation with Eth in AILI also attenuates the downregulation of PLPP2 (Supplementary Fig. 4i). Therefore, during the injury phase of ALI, a feedback loop involving PE-XBP1-PLPP2-PE exacerbated liver injury (Supplementary Fig. 4j). Similarly, during the repair phase of ALI, we observed that the resolution of ER stress induced by Plpp2 overexpression could be blocked by pharmacological inhibition of PE synthesis (Supplementary Fig. 4k–n). These findings demonstrate that the PE-XBP1-PLPP2-PE circuit, which reflects the intricate interplay between phospholipid metabolism and ER stress, is operative throughout the entire course of ALI and plays an indispensable role in disease pathogenesis and resolution. PLPP2 functions as a critical regulatory node that integrates ER stress with phospholipid homeostasis.

Pharmacological activation of PLPP2 promotes liver repair and regeneration after ALI
To evaluate the therapeutic potential of PLPP2 agonists in ALI, we performed virtual screening to identify natural compounds capable of binding to PLPP2. Based on docking affinity analyses, we selected the top 10 compounds with the lowest affinity energies and further assessed their effects on PLPP2-mediated PE synthesis (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Among these, Pregnenolone monosulfate (HY-110189) exhibited the most potent activation of PLPP2 in PE biosynthesis (Fig. 8a). By purifying the PLPP2 protein, we have clearly demonstrated that HY-110189 can enhance the dephosphorylation activity of PLPP2 toward its substrate PA27 (Fig. 8b, c). Molecular docking analyses confirmed the direct binding between PLPP2 and HY-110189 (Fig. 8d), while molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated the structural stability and dynamic interactions of the PLPP2-HY-110189 complex at the atomic level (Fig. 8e and Supplementary Fig. 8b,c). In addition, Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA) and WB experiments confirmed the direct binding interaction between HY-110189 and PLPP2 (Fig. 8f, g). In vivo validation studies revealed that HY-110189 significantly ameliorated AILI (Fig. 8h, i). Notably, the protective effects of HY-110189 were abolished in Plpp2ΔHep mice, confirming its mechanism of action (Fig. 8j, k). Mechanistic studies indicated that HY110189 actually influenced autophagy and the Hedgehog signaling pathway by activating the PLPP2-PE axis (Fig. 8l, m). Furthermore, PLPP2 activation by HY110189 also conferred protective effects against CCL4- and lR-induced liver injury (Fig. 8n, o).
