paper.title: Phospholipid phosphatase 2 drives liver repair and regeneration after acute liver injury.
paper.abstract: Acute liver injury is commonly caused by overdose-drug, toxins, or ischemia. The liver possesses a remarkable regenerative capacity, wherein metabolic remodeling plays a crucial role in restoring hepatic function and homeostasis. However, the specific metabolic shift that initiates hepatocyte regeneration remains unclear. Here, we employed multi-time-point multi-omics analyses to demonstrate that phosphatidylethanolamine undergoes a dynamic metabolic reprogramming, with phospholipid phosphatase 2 (PLPP2) exhibiting synchronous changes among the enzymes regulating PE metabolism. Liver biopsy samples from patients with drug-induced liver injury corroborated the PLPP2 alterations. In murine models, hepatocyte-specific deletion of PLPP2 exacerbated acute liver injury. Mechanistically, the resolution of ER stress was accompanied by a robust upregulation of PLPP2 during the regenerative phase. This shift promotes liver repair and regeneration by initiating the PE biosynthesis. PE, upon binding to PEBP1, modulated its affinity and strengthened its interaction with GLI1, thereby disrupting the association between lTCH and GLI1 and preventing the ubiquitination and degradation of GLI1. Additionally, PE promotes autophagy by facilitating the lipidation of LC3B. The increase in ER-localized PE mediated by PLPP2 also contributed to the alleviation of ER stress, thus establishing a positive feedback loop. Pharmacologic activation of PLPP2 or supplementation with ethanolamine may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for acute liver injury.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Acute liver injury (ALI) is a clinically significant condition characterized by the rapid onset of hepatocellular damage, leading to impaired liver function within days or weeks. It is typically triggered by factors such as drug toxicity (most notably acetaminophen (APAP) overdose, which is the leading cause of drug-induced liver injury (DILI)) as well as viral hepatitis, ischemia, or autoimmune responses.1 ALI is associated with elevated transaminase levels, coagulopathy, and, in severe cases, acute liver failure (ALF).1 Given its role as a leading cause of hepatic emergencies and high mortality in fulminant cases, studying ALI is a critical clinical imperative. The rapid progression from hepatocyte necrosis to systemic inflammatory response syndrome and multi-organ dysfunction syndrome creates a narrow therapeutic window. Current management remains largely supportive, lacking specific agents to halt the cycle of regulated cell death. Therefore, focused research is essential to develop targeted therapies. This will enable the discovery of early biomarkers and effective treatments, reducing reliance on liver transplantation and improving survival.

ALI exhibits a biphasic progression, characterized by an initial phase of innate immune activation and hepatocyte damage, followed by a repair phase marked by inflammation resolution and hepatocyte regeneration.2–4 Previous studies have demonstrated that metabolic reprogramming serves as a critical adaptive mechanism for mitigating ALI. Pericentral hepatocytes upregulate asparagine synthetase expression, converting glutamine to asparagine to aid hepatoprotection.5 Additionally, elevated Mas receptor activity in hepatocytes promotes lipophagy and fatty acid oxidation via the AKT-FOXO1 pathway, alleviating APAP-induced acute liver injury (AILI).6 These findings underscore how tailored metabolic adaptations act as endogenous protective strategies. However, the precise metabolic shift driving liver regeneration after ALI remains poorly defined. Identifying these key mechanisms may provide novel therapeutic targets for enhancing liver recovery.

Emerging evidence from multiple organ systems has increasingly underscored the critical role of phospholipid metabolism in orchestrating tissue regeneration. Specifically, a growing body of research has established that sphingolipid metabolism is indispensable for cardiac regeneration in mammals, as it modulates key proliferative and survival signals in cardiomyocytes.7 In parallel, the regulation of glycerolipid metabolism within neurons has been shown to critically dictate the extent and success of axonal regrowth and functional recovery following central nervous system injury.8 Consistent with these cross-tissue observations, recent preclinical work has revealed that either exogenous phosphatidic acid (PA) administration or pharmacological activation of the anabolic cardiolipin synthesis pathway attenuates ALl and enhances hepatocyte regeneration in mice.9 Collectively, these data point toward a compelling concept: the dynamic regulation of phospholipid metabolism may constitute a phylogenetically conserved, fundamental mechanism that governs the efficiency of tissue repair and regeneration across a wide spectrum of biological contexts.

Phospholipids, encompassing major classes such as phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and other related lipid species, are not only fundamental structural constituents of cellular membranes but also serve as critical mediators of membrane dynamics, intracellular signaling transduction, and overall cellular metabolism.10 Although previous studies have firmly established that PE and its associated autophagy play important roles in the contexts of aging and cancer,11,12 the specific contribution and functional significance of PE in the pathophysiology of ALI remain remarkably underexplored and poorly defined. In this study, we employed multi-timepoint multi-omics approaches to, for the first time, systematically delineate and demonstrate that PE metabolism is indispensable for hepatic repair and regeneration following ALI. Further investigations identified phospholipid phosphatase 2 (PLPP2) as a key metabolic enzyme mediating PE biosynthesis in the context of ALI and regulating hepatic repair and regeneration. Functional studies demonstrated that PE synthesized by PLPP2 not only promoted liver repair via the well-characterized autophagy pathway but also prevented the ubiquitination of GLI1 via altering the affinity of PE binding protein 1 (PEBP1), thereby regulating hepatocyte regeneration. Taken together, these integrated findings definitively establish PLPP2 as a promising and previously unrecognized therapeutic target for accelerating recovery from ALI.

Multi-timepoint and multi-omics analyses uncover dynamic remodeling of phospholipid metabolism following AILI
To investigate the dynamic changes in ALI and elucidate the molecular mechanisms governing hepatocyte regeneration, we performed proteomic analysis of liver tissues and hepatic enzyme assay of peripheral blood collected at multiple time points post-APAP treatment (Fig. 1a, b and Supplementary Fig. 1a, c). Unsupervised clustering analysis of the proteomic data revealed distinct temporal patterns, with high similarity observed between the 0 h and 168 h time points (representing pre- and post-injury baselines), the 6 h and 24 h time points (acute injury phase), and the 48 h, 72 h, and 96 h time points (recovery phase) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Further classification of all differentially expressed proteins into eight distinct clusters based on their temporal expression trajectories identified unique protein expression patterns in the entire process (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Heatmaps revealed significant upregulation of proteins involved in the apoptotic, necrotic, and inflammatory pathways within 48 h post-APAP (Fig. 1c). These findings were corroborated by histopathological evidence of hepatocellular death and inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 1d), as well as elevated serum ALT and AST levels (Fig. 1b). It supports the hypothesis that the injury phase predominantly occurs within the first 48 h post-APAP.Fig. 1Multi-timepoint and multi-omics analyses uncover dynamic remodeling of phospholipid metabolism following AILI. a Schematic diagram of liver tissues collection from mice at seven time points following AILI. Proteomics and metabolomics were integrated to delineate the entire temporal progression-from injury to repair. b Serum ALT and AST levels assayed by ELISA at indicated time points post APAP (n = 6, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). c Heat maps show expression of members of apoptosis, necrosis and inflammation pathways (n = 3, proteomics). d Representative gross liver photographs and intrahepatic staining with quantification of H&E (necrotic areas circled with white lines), TUNEL (apoptosis) (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). e Heat map shows expression of the cell proliferation pathway (n = 3, proteomics). f Immunohistochemical staining with quantification of mouse liver tissues for Ki67 and PCNA (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, **p < 0.01; ****p < 0.0001). g Representative FCM plots and quantification of MoMFs, KCs, and neutrophils in mouse liver tissues at indicated time points post APAP (n = 3, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). h The changes of APAP-related metabolites in metabolomics (n = 6, metabolomics). i The intersection of enriched pathways from multi-omics analysis for three couples, including 48 h vs 6 h, 72 h vs 6 h, and 96 h vs 6 h. j The pathways co-enriched by proteomics and metabolomics at 48 h and 6 h after APAP

The liver entered the repair phase at 48 h post-APAP. During this stage, the expression of proteins associated with cell proliferation was markedly upregulated (Fig. 1e), as further corroborated by immunohistochemical staining for the proliferative markers Ki67 and PCNA (Fig. 1f). Consistently, both KEGG pathway analysis and GSEA demonstrated significant enrichment and upregulation of cell proliferation-related pathways at 48 h post-APAP (Supplementary Fig. 1e–g).

To comprehensively characterize the dynamic inflammatory response throughout the course of ALI, we performed liver perfusions at seven time points and analyzed non-parenchymal cells via flow cytometry (FCM). Kupffer cells sharply decreased during liver injury but recovered to baseline after repair completion. In contrast, neutrophils and infiltrating macrophages (iMФs) surged during injury and declined during repair. Notably, Ly6Chigh iMФs gradually shifted to Ly6Clow iMФs as the liver transitioned from injury to repair3,13 (Fig. 1g). The transition from a pro-inflammatory to an anti-inflammatory microenvironment paralleled the aforementioned hepatocellular regeneration.

These results collectively indicate that 48 h post-APAP constitutes a critical temporal window during which the liver undergoes a phenotypic transition from injury to regeneration.

To investigate metabolic alterations following ALI, we also conducted an untargeted metabolomic profiling analysis using liver tissues collected from mice euthanized at seven time points post-APAP (Supplementary Fig. 1h, j). Consistent with the findings shown in Fig. 1, the metabonomic heatmaps at 0, 72, 96, and 168 h exhibited high similarity, whereas those at 6, 24, and 48 h demonstrated moderate similarity (Supplementary Fig. 1h). Based on the temporal dynamics of these differential metabolites, they were systematically grouped into eight distinct metabolic subtypes, thereby identifying characteristic metabolic transition patterns during the entire process (Supplementary Fig. 1i). Furthermore, hepatic APAP concentration peaked at 6 h post-APAP and subsequently declined gradually. Conversely, the glutathione (GSH) levels exhibited an inverse temporal pattern (Fig. 1h). To identify the key metabolic remodeling pathway driving liver regeneration, we performed an integrated proteomic and metabolomic analysis. Given that 6 h and 24 h time points represented the injury phase, while 48,72, and 96 h correspond to the repair phase, we analyzed the overlapping enriched pathways between not only H48 vs. H6, H72 vs. H6 and H96 vs. H6 but also H48 vs. H24, H72 vs. H24 and H96 vs. H24 (Fig. 1i and Supplementary Fig. 1k). The results demonstrated that the autophagy pathway was significantly enriched for the metabolite PE during the repair phase (Fig. 1j and Supplementary Fig. 1l). Previous studies have demonstrated that PE constitutes the predominant phospholipid component of autophagosome membranes, where it covalently conjugates with LC3 protein to form LC3-II (PE-LC3 complex), thereby facilitating autophagosome membrane elongation and closure.14 Therefore, we hypothesize that autophagy-associated metabolite PE exerts critical regulatory functions during the regenerative process.

PE exerts a protective effect against ALI
Initially, we assessed the temporal dynamics of autophagy. Immunofluorescence staining of LC3B and P62 in mouse liver tissues, along with Western blot (WB) analysis of LC3B expression, revealed a downregulation of autophagy during the injury phase, followed by its upregulation during the repair phase (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2a). The heatmap of autophagy-related proteins in the proteomic analysis further validated this dynamic regulation during AILI (Fig. 2b). Conversely, the autophagy substrate P62 exhibited an inverse expression pattern (Fig. 2c). These findings clearly demonstrate that autophagy plays a crucial role in liver repair.Fig. 2PE exerts a protective effect against ALI. a Representative intrahepatic staining and quantification of LC3B and P62 (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 6, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). b Heat map shows expression of autophagy pathway (n = 3, proteomics). c The abundance change of Sqstm1 (P62) (n = 3, proteomics). d Heat map shows the level of PE (n = 6, metabolomics). e PE levels of mouse liver tissues assayed by ELISA (n = 10, two-tailed Student’s t test, **p < 0.01; ****p < 0.0001). f Schematic diagram of phospholipid metabolism. g Correlation between PE levels of mouse liver tissues and serum ALT & AST levels (two-tailed Pearson’s test). h Schematic diagram of PBS or Etn administration (20 mg/kg). i PE levels of mouse liver tissues assayed by ELISA after PBS or Etn administration (n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). j Representative liver photographs and intrahepatic staining with quantification of H&E, Ki67, LC3B, and P62 (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t-test, ****p < 0.0001). k, l Representative intrahepatic staining with quantification of H&E and Ki67 after CCL4 (0.6 ml/kg, dissolved in olive oil)- or IR-induced liver injury (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 6, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001)

Furthermore, the metabolic heatmap confirmed that PE underwent distinct metabolic remodeling (Fig. 2d). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) quantification of hepatic PE levels yielded consistent result (Fig. 2e). A previous study has reported that in the early phase of liver regeneration following partial hepatectomy, lipids, including PE, are markedly enriched.15 In our study, a negative correlation was observed between hepatic PE content and serum ALT and AST levels at 48 h post-APAP, indicating a potential protective role of PE against ALI (Fig. 2g). Pharmacological supplementation with ethanolamine (Etn), a precursor for PE synthesis (Fig. 2f), attenuated AILI and enhanced autophagy (Fig. 2h–j and Supplementary Fig. 2b). Similarly, elevated PE levels demonstrated protective effects in CCL4- and ischemia-reperfusion (lR)-induced liver injury models, where autophagy was also vital for liver repair16,17 (Fig. 2k, l). Consistently, Etn exhibited a parallel trend in metabolic flux, suggesting its role in providing substrate support for PE biosynthesis. (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 2c). Collectively, these findings suggest that PE metabolism is dynamically upregulated and promotes liver repair during the recovery phase of ALI.

The upregulation of PLPP2 and the increase of PE occur synchronously in time
To elucidate the regulatory mechanism underlying PE metabolic reprogramming in ALI, we analyzed the expression dynamics of key PE-metabolizing enzymes across the entire continuum (Figs. 2f, 3a). Among these, PLPP2 exhibited the most pronounced differential expression, demonstrating a temporal expression pattern that closely paralleled the metabolic remodeling of PE (Fig. 3a, b). Furthermore, both mRNA and protein levels of PLPP2 of mouse liver tissues (primary hepatocytes) or THLE-2 cells showed a significant downregulation during the injury phase followed by a robust upregulation during the repair phase (Fig. 3c, d and Supplementary Fig. 3a, b). Immunohistochemical analysis of liver tissues and immunofluorescence staining of THLE-2 cells corroborated these expression patterns (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. 3c–e). Collectively, these results suggest that PLPP2 upregulation likely mediates the elevated PE levels during the regenerative phase.Fig. 3The upregulation of PLPP2, regulated by XBP1, is synchronized with the metabolic skew of PE in time. a Volcano plot of proteins differently expressed in three couples including 48 h vs 6 h,72 h vs 6 h and 96 h vs 6 h (n = 3, proteomics). b The abundance change of Plpp2 (n = 3, proteomics). c, d PLPP2 mRNA expression and protein expression of primary hepatocytes sorted from mouse liver tissues or THLE-2 cells at indicated time points post APAP (n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). e Representative histological staining of PLPP2 in mouse liver tissues at the indicated time points post APAP (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8). f Correlation between Plpp2 mRNA expression of mouse liver tissues and serum ALT & AST levels (two-tailed Pearson’s test). g Schematic diagram of human liver samples collection. h Representative immunohistochemical staining of PLPP2 in human liver samples obtained from HC (n = 31) and DILI (n = 36) groups (Scale bars, 50 μm. HC-1 to −5 and DILI-1 to −5 represent individual patient samples from healthy controls and drug-induced liver injury patients, respectively). i Quantification of PLPP2 in human liver samples obtained from HC (n = 31) and DILI (n = 36) groups (****p < 0.0001). j Quantification of Ki67 in human liver samples from PLPP2high group and PLPP2low group (n = 18, two-tailed Student’s t test, **p < 0.01). k Representative intrahepatic staining of PLPP2 and HNF4a in human liver samples(Scale bars, 50 μm). l The intersection of PLPP2 transcription factors predicted by Database. m Integrative genomics viewer (IGV) analysis representing XBP1 peaks at the PLPP2 loci. n The online tool JASPAR was used to predict potential binding sites near the PLPP2 transcriptional start site. o Luciferase reporter assays for binding site deletion or site-directed mutagenesis in HepG2 cells following XBP1 knockdown or overexpression (n = 5, two-tailed Student’s t test, ns p > 0.05; ****p < 0.0001). p ChIP assays in HepG2 cells to investigate the binding of XBP1 to the PLPP2 promoter sequences (n = 5, two-tailed Student’s t test, ns p > 0.05; ****p < 0.0001). q Representative confocal microscopy images of HepG2 cells after APAP stained with PLPP2 (green) and XBP1 (red) (Scale bars, 10 μm)

Simultaneously, we quantified hepatic Plpp2 mRNA levels and the levels of serum ALT&AST, where a significant negative correlation was observed (Fig. 3f). Based on these findings, we hypothesize that PLPP2 may exert a protective effect against AILI.

Patients with DILI exhibiting higher PLPP2 expression in liver tissues demonstrate significantly better prognosis
More objectively, we collected liver samples from patients with hepatic hemangioma as healthy controls (HC) and DILI for PLPP2 expression analysis (Fig. 3g). Notably, hepatocyte PLPP2 was markedly upregulated in DILl specimens compared to that in HC (Fig. 3h, i, k). lmportantly, patients exhibiting higher PLPP2 expression displayed higher Ki67 levels (Fig. 3j). Meanwhile, we also collected peripheral blood from patients with DILI and measured the levels of liver enzymes. We found that a higher expression of PLPP2 was associated with lower liver enzymes (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Therefore, we hypothesized that PLPP2 played an important protective role in ALI.

XBP1 transcriptionally regulates the expression of PLPP2 in ALI
To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying PLPP2 upregulation, we first investigated transcriptional regulation. Using the JASPAR and KnockTF databases, and based on sequence motif analysis and known regulatory relationships in the databases, we identified six potential transcription factors that may regulate the expression of PLPP2 (Fig. 3l). Among these, X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) was reported to be significantly upregulated in ALI, a finding consistent with our immunofluorescence data (Supplementary Fig. 3g). Moreover, hepatocyte-specific deletion of XBP1 attenuated ALI.18,19 Our previous studies on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) demonstrated that hepatic XBP1 expression is markedly upregulated and accelerates the progression of chronic inflammation through its regulatory role in lipid metabolism.20 Based on these findings, we hypothesize that XBP1 may transcriptionally suppress PLPP2 expression, thereby influencing PE metabolism. This hypothesis was validated by Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag), which showed that XBP1 bound to the PLPP2 promoter at 6 h post-APAP, while binding decreased at 48 h post-APAP (Fig. 3m). Subsequently, the online tool JASPAR was used to predict potential XBP1 binding sites (BS) in the PLPP2 promoter, revealing three putative binding sites (Fig. 3n and Supplementary Fig. 3h). Dual-luciferase reporter assays and ChlP assays demonstrated that BS1 is essential for the transcriptional inhibition of PLPP2 by XBP1, which was also verified by the immunofluorescence staining of HepG2 cells (Fig. 3o–q and Supplementary Fig. 3i). Further investigation revealed that both PLPP2 protein level and hepatic PE content were significantly elevated in Xbp1ΔHep mice, which promoted liver repair (Supplementary Fig. 3j–l). Thus, we infer that XBP1 modulates PLPP2 expression in ALI, thereby regulating PE biosynthesis.

PLPP2 acts as a pivotal regulatory hub integrating endoplasmic reticulum stress and phospholipid metabolism
To further validate the functional role of PLPP2 in ALI, we generated hepatocyte-specific Plpp2 knockout mice (Plpp2ΔHep) and hepatocyte-specific Plpp2 overexpression mice (AAV-Plpp2) (Supplementary Fig. 9a–e). Literature reports that the phospholipid composition within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) modulates ER stress through the regulation of unfolded protein.21 Interestingly, ER stress was significantly upregulated following Plpp2 knockout according to transcriptomic data (Supplementary Fig. 4a–c). We hypothesized that Plpp2 deficiency led to reduced ER PE levels, thereby inducing ER stress. The expression of ER stress-related genes at both the mRNA and protein levels supported the induction of ER stress by Plpp2 deficiency in AILI, while supplementation with Etn alleviated ER stress. Immunofluorescence staining results were consistent with these findings (Supplementary Fig. 4d–h). Furthermore, supplementation with Eth in AILI also attenuates the downregulation of PLPP2 (Supplementary Fig. 4i). Therefore, during the injury phase of ALI, a feedback loop involving PE-XBP1-PLPP2-PE exacerbated liver injury (Supplementary Fig. 4j). Similarly, during the repair phase of ALI, we observed that the resolution of ER stress induced by Plpp2 overexpression could be blocked by pharmacological inhibition of PE synthesis (Supplementary Fig. 4k–n). These findings demonstrate that the PE-XBP1-PLPP2-PE circuit, which reflects the intricate interplay between phospholipid metabolism and ER stress, is operative throughout the entire course of ALI and plays an indispensable role in disease pathogenesis and resolution. PLPP2 functions as a critical regulatory node that integrates ER stress with phospholipid homeostasis.

Hepatocyte PLPP2 governs liver repair and regeneration after ALI
Notably, Plpp2ΔHep mice exhibited a dramatic increase in serum ALT and AST levels compared with Plpp2FL/FL controls at 48 h post-APAP (Fig. 4b). Conversely, AAV-Plpp2 mice exhibited serum ALT and AST levels closer to normal than AAV-GFP mice (Fig. 4c). Furthermore, in a survival assay using a lethal dose of APAP, Plpp2ΔHep mice showed significantly reduced survival rate, whereas AAV-Plpp2 mice exhibited a significantly higher survival rate (Fig. 4d, e). Consistently, H&E staining revealed enlarged necrotic areas in the livers of Plpp2ΔHep mice, accompanied by a significant reduction in Ki67 (Fig. 4f, g). However, AAV-Plpp2 mice showed the opposite results (Fig. 4h, i). To further validate the correlation between PLPP2 and Ki67, we performed dual-immunofluorescence staining, which showed a strong positive association (Fig. 4j–n). This result was verified by transcriptomics data (Fig. 4o). To validate the restorative effect, Plpp2-overexpressing adenovirus was administered to Plpp2ΔHep mice, and H&E staining results showed that Plpp2 overexpression effectively counteracted the exacerbation of liver injury caused by Plpp2 deficiency (Supplementary Fig. 5g). Furthermore, in partial hepatectomy models as well as in CCL4- and I/R-induced liver injury models, hepatocyte-specific Plpp2 deficiency delayed liver regeneration and repair (Fig. 4p–s).Fig. 4Hepatocyte PLPP2 governs liver regeneration after ALI. a Schematic diagram of the study for the role and mechanism of PLPP2 in APAP-induced liver injury. Transcriptomics and metabonomics were employed to validate the role of PLPP2. Natural compounds targeting PLPP2 were subjected to virtual screening. b Serum ALT and AST levels in Plpp2FL/FL and Plpp2ΔHep mice treated with APAP (300 mg/kg) for 48 h (n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). c Serum ALT and AST levels in AAV-GFP and AAV-Plpp2 mice treated with APAP (300 mg/kg) for 48 h (n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). d Survival curves of Plpp2FL/FL and Plpp2ΔHep mice treated with a lethal dose of APAP (650 mg/kg) (n = 20, log-rank test). e Survival curves of AAV-GFP and AAV-Plpp2 mice treated with a lethal dose of APAP (650 mg/kg) (n = 20, log-rank test). f–i Representative gross liver photographs and intrahepatic staining with quantification of H&E and Ki67 (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). j–m Representative co-staining and quantification of PLPP2/Ki67 (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 8, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). n Correlation between PLPP2 expression and Ki67 expression in mouse liver tissues (two-tailed Pearson’s test). o Heat map shows expression of members of Apoptosis and Cell Proliferation pathways (n = 3, transcriptomics). p Representative intrahepatic staining with quantification of Ki67 in Plpp2FL/FL, Plpp2ΔHep, AAV-GFP and AAV-Plpp2 mice after 70% partial hepatectomy (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 5, two-tailed Student’s t test, ****p < 0.0001). q Liver-to-body weight ratio of Plpp2FL/FL, Plpp2ΔHep, AAV-GFP and AAV-Plpp2 mice 36 h after 70% PHx (n = 5, two-tailed Student’s t test, ***p < 0.001). r, s Representative intrahepatic staining with quantification of H&E and Ki67 in Plpp2FL/FL and Plpp2ΔHep mice after CCL4 (0.6 ml/kg, dissolved in olive oil)- or IR-induced liver injury (Scale bars, 50 μm. n = 6, two-tailed Student’s t test, ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001)

We also generated an adenovirus that specifically targeted hepatocyte-specific Plpp2 (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). Importantly, after establishing the ALI model, we obtained results that were identical to those observed in Plpp2ΔHep mice (Supplementary Fig. 5c–f). These data suggest that PLPP2 orchestrates liver repair and regeneration following ALI.

PLPP2 promotes liver repair by enhancing autophagy via upregulation of PE
The hepatoprotective effect of PLPP2 in ALI has been established. However, the precise molecular mechanism by which PLPP2 governs hepatocyte regeneration remains unclear. PLPP2 dephosphorylates PA to produce diacylglycerol (DAG), which subsequently participates in the CDP-ethanolamine pathway for PE biosynthesis22 (Fig. 2f). Our results demonstrated that Plpp2 deficiency downregulated the autophagy marker LC3B and upregulated the autophagic substrate P62 (Fig. 5e). Immunofluorescence staining of mouse liver tissues and THLE-2 cells demonstrated concordant findings (Fig. 5h–m and Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Furthermore, transcriptomic data revealed that Plpp2 deletion led to an increase in P62, accompanied by upregulation of autophagy-related genes, which we speculated that might have a feedback regulatory mechanism (Fig. 5s). Intriguingly, PEBP1 was found to physically associate with GLI1, a key transcription factor in the Hedgehog pathway, specifically under Plpp2-overexpressing or Etn supplementation conditions (Fig. 6h, i). To validate this interaction, we generated FLAG-tagged PEBP1 and His-tagged GLI1 constructs, which were co-expressed in HEK293T cells. Meanwhile, molecular docking analyses revealed that PEBP1 also bound to the Transcription-activation domain (D3: residues 554–1106) of GLI1 (Fig. 6o). Discussion
ALI is an acute-onset disease characterized by a biphasic clinical course.2 Previous studies have primarily focused on the uniphasic phase (either injury or repair). Here, we pioneered the application of multi-time-point, multi-omics approaches to perform a comprehensive, multi-dimensional analysis of ALI, enabling the precise identification of key regulatory molecules throughout the entire trajectory.

Our previous studies have elucidated the critical role of macrophages in regulating the activation and resolution of inflammatory responses in acute and chronic liver inflammatory diseases.20,28,29 However, the mechanisms underlying intrinsic hepatocyte regeneration and repair remain poorly defined.

We first identified 48 h post-APAP as the critical time point at which hepatocytes transition from injury to repair. Subsequent combined metabolomic studies revealed that phospholipid metabolism becomes significantly activated during the repair phase, with PE metabolism being particularly prominent. Previous studies have demonstrated that dioleoyl-phosphatidylethanolamine supplementation in necrotizing enterocolitis protects intestinal barrier function by inhibiting ferroptosis.30 Similarly, accelerating PE synthesis in MASH similarly attenuates lipotoxicity.31,32 The biological effects of PE depend on its subclass composition, subcellular or tissue distribution, metabolic context, and the balance between its biosynthesis and degradation. Under physiological conditions or controlled supplementation, PE exerts protective effects by maintaining membrane stability, providing antioxidant defense, facilitating lipid transport, and preserving mitochondrial integrity. Conversely, in pathological states (metabolic dysregulation, nutrient deficiency, or oxidative stress overload), excessive or imbalanced PE accumulation can exacerbate membrane damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and hepatocellular apoptosis, leading to loss of its protective role and even promoting cellular injury.33 A classic example is methionine- and choline-deficient (MCD) diet-induced MASH, where abnormal PE accumulation triggers reactive oxygen species (ROS) buildup that damages mitochondrial membranes, exacerbating mitochondrial dysfunction, hepatocyte apoptosis.34 In our study, supporting evidence from Etn supplementation studies demonstrated that increased hepatic PE content confers protective effects on ALI. Subsequently, through systematic analysis of the expression dynamics of all PE-metabolizing enzymes, it was revealed that PLPP2 exhibited temporal and quantitative correlation with PE levels.

PLPP2 has been implicated in tumor cell proliferation.35–37 Furthermore, its family member PLPP3 has been proven to regulate vascular repair and functional recovery following stroke.38 We observed a marked upregulation of PLPP2 expression in liver samples of humans with DILI. To investigate the functional role of PLPP2, we generated Plpp2ΔHep mice and AAV-Plpp2 mice. Our findings demonstrate that PLPP2 exerts hepatoprotective effects by enhancing PE biosynthesis.

Notably, the biogenesis, elongation, and membrane sealing of autophagosomal membranes exhibit a critical dependency on PE availability.39 Moreover, hepatocyte autophagy has been established as a protective mechanism in ALI.40,41 Here, we provide the first evidence that PLPP2 enhances autophagy by increasing PE synthesis, thereby accelerating liver repair.

PE is also reported to bind to and modulate the conformational state of PEBP1, altering its binding specificity.23 Our study demonstrates for the first time that PLPP2-driven PE metabolism reprogramming enhances the interaction between PEBP1 and the transcription factor GLI1, thereby stabilizing GLI1 and activating the Hedgehog signaling pathway to promote hepatocyte regeneration. This work uncovers a novel mechanism whereby the lipid-metabolizing enzyme PLPP2 regulates developmental signaling through metabolite-protein interaction networks.

PA, as a substrate of PLPP2, can activate inflammatory responses.42 Our experiments confirmed, consistent with the previous report,9 that PA supplementation attenuates injury; however, Plpp2 deficiency abrogated this protective effect (Unshown Data). Thus, PLPP2 exerts a dual protective mechanism in ALI by not only enhancing the autophagy-mediated resolution of inflammation but also modulating PA levels.43

PE is predominantly synthesized in the ER, where it constitutes the major phospholipid component of the ER membrane.44 This enrichment is indispensable for maintaining ER membrane integrity and functionality, particularly for supporting lipid bilayer dynamics and protein folding processes. Impaired PE biosynthesis disrupts these homeostatic mechanisms, thereby inducing ER stress.21 ER stress signaling exhibits significant upregulation during the injury phase of ALI, followed by a gradual downregulation during the repair phase. Targeted inhibition of XBP1 markedly alleviates liver injury.18 Interestingly, the expression pattern of XBP1 exhibits a reciprocal relationship with that of PLPP2. Our findings demonstrate that XBP1 transcriptionally suppresses PLPP2 expression, thereby uncovering a novel regulatory link between ER stress and phospholipid metabolism. During the injury phase, PE biosynthesis deficiency induces ER stress, which subsequently suppresses PE synthesis. Conversely, during the repair phase, enhanced PE synthesis attenuates ER stress, thereby further promoting PE production and creating a pro-regenerative feedback loop that facilitates liver recovery. PLPP2 serves as a central regulator in feedback loop, critically modulating this dynamic balance. Overall, the re-equilibration of phospholipid homeostasis following ALI serves as a biochemical mirror that reflects the transition from injury to regeneration.

In summary, our study reveals that hepatocyte PLPP2 serves as a critical regulator of liver repair and regeneration after ALI. Pharmacological activation or overexpression of PLPP2 not only promotes hepatocyte autophagy through PE lipidation of LC3B, accelerating liver repair, but also stabilizes GLI1 via the PE-PEBP1 axis, accelerating hepatocyte regeneration. These results identify hepatocyte PLPP2 as a key molecular switch that directs hepatocytes from injury toward regeneration by orchestrating PE metabolism. Consequently, targeted activation of PLPP2 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of ALI in clinical practice. Although we have screened agonists of PLPP2 and evaluated its effect, it remains unclear whether the agent acts specifically on liver or whether it also influences other organ systems. Moreover, supplementing Etn in patients with ALI following surgery also represents a highly promising direction. However, several challenges remain, including the need to define its safety profile, determine the optimal route and dosage of administration, and assess long-term effects. We are confident that stepwise progress in addressing these issues will open new avenues for the treatment of ALI.

Human liver samples
Human liver samples were collected from 36 patients with DILI who underwent percutaneous liver biopsy in the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. Furthermore, 31 patients without DILI (patients with hepatic hemangioma) were used as normal controls from the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. Informed consent was obtained from each subject. The study was carried out under the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the research ethics boards of the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (2025-SR-423). Demographic features of enrolled subjects are shown in Table S1.

Mice and Mouse Models
The wild-type (WT), FloxP-Plpp2 (PlppFL/FL), Alb-Cre Plpp2 knockout (Plpp2ΔHep), FloxP-Xbp1 (Xbp1FL/FL), and Alb-Cre Xbp1 knockout (Xbp1ΔHep) mice used in this study were obtained from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. For the liver-specific silencing of Plpp2, AAV2/8-TBG-EGFP-Plpp2-shRNA717 vs AAV2/8-TBG-EGFP-Scramble adenoviruses (Genomeditech (Shanghai) Co.,Ltd) were pre-delivered via tail vein injection at a dose of 10*1012 vg/kg, 28 days prior to APAP challenge. For the liver-specific overexpression of Plpp2, AAV2/8-TBG-Plpp2-EGFP vs. AAV2/8-TBG-EGFP adenoviruses (Genomeditech (Shanghai) Co.,Ltd) were pre-delivered via tail vein injection at a dose of 10*1012 vg/kg, 28 days prior to APAP (MCE, HY-66005) challenge. Littermate controls were used where appropriate. All mouse strains had a C57BL/6 J genetic background, were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions, maintained on a 12-hour light/dark cycle, and had free access to water and standard chow. All animals were treated humanely, and all procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Nanjing Medical University.

To develop the AILI model, 8–10-week-old male mice were either given an intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of 300 mg/kg (or lethal dose 650 mg/kg) APAP, following overnight fasting. Unless specified, ethanolamine (Etn,20 mg/kg; MCE, HY-Y0524) or meclizine (Mec,50 mg/kg; MCE, HY-B0349A) was intraperitoneally injected into mice 24 h after APAP. SAG (10 mg/kg; MCE, HY-12848), GANT-61 (40 mg/kg; MCE, HY-13901), Rapamycin (RAPA, 2 mg/kg; MCE, HY-10219) or chloroquine (CQ, 60 mg/kg; MCE, HY-17589A) was intraperitoneally injected into mice 24 h after APAP. HY-110189(10 mg/kg; MCE) was intraperitoneally injected into mice 2 h after APAP. To induce CCL4-induced liver injury, 8–10-week-old mice received one intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection (0.6 ml/kg body weight) of carbon tetrachloride (CCL4) (Sigma-Aldrich, 87030) diluted 1/10 in olive oil.45 To generate the 70% HIRI model, following anesthesia and a median abdominal incision, the portal vein and hepatic artery of the left and median hepatic lobes were occluded using a microvascular clamp. After 60 minutes of ischemia, the clamp was removed, and the mice were sacrificed after 72 h of reperfusion.46 To generate the PHx model, 8-10-week-old male mice were subjected to 70% partial hepatectomy, as described previously.45 Mice were sacrificed for analyses at the indicated time points, except for non-experimental related death or developing diseases that may affect the experimental results. All animal experiments were conducted in the experimental operation room of Jiangsu Provincial Laboratory Animal Center.

Isolation of hepatocytes
Hepatocytes from mice were isolated by two-step collagenase perfusion. In brief, livers were perfused in situ via the portal vein with 50 ml warmed (37 °C) Hanks’ balanced salt solution (Ca2+ and Mg2+ free) containing EGTA (0.5 M), followed by collagenase IV (Sigma, 0.05% w/v, dissolved in HBSS with Ca2+ and Mg2+). Perfused livers were dissected and teased through 70-mm nylon mesh cell strainers. Hepatocytes were separated by an initial centrifugation at 50×g for 3 min.

Protein expression and purification
PLPP2-GFP fusion protein expression plasmid was generated and transiently transfected into HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen). 48 h post-transfection, cells were harvested and resuspended in ice-cold lysis buffer (Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, supplemented with protease inhibitors). Cell lysis was performed by sonication, and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation. The resulting supernatant contained the GFP-tagged PLPP2 protein.

To purify the fusion protein, the supernatant was incubated with Sepharose 4B agarose beads covalently coupled to a high-affinity GFP monoclonal antibody at 4 °C under gentle agitation for 2 h. After extensive washing with an acidic pre-wash buffer, the bound protein was eluted using a pH 3.0 Arginine-HCl solution and immediately neutralized with a neutral buffer. The eluate was concentrated and further purified by size exclusion chromatography. Fractions corresponding to the major peak were pooled and concentrated prior to downstream applications.

Enzyme activity assay
The enzymatic activity was measured following the protocol described in an article published in Nature Chemical Biology.27 First, a reaction mixture was prepared containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 100 µM substrate PA, and 8.3 mM Triton X-100. To 89 µL of the reaction mixture, 1 µL of PLPP2 purified protein (0.03 mg/mL) was added. Then, the reaction was incubated at 37 °C for 20 min, and enzyme activity was determined using the malachite green ammonium molybdate assay.

Cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA)
THLE-2 cell lysates were divided into two aliquots: one was kept as a control, and the other was treated with 20 µM HY-110189 for 1 hour at room temperature. Both aliquots were then heated at designated temperatures (50–85 °C) for 5 minutes, followed by cooling to room temperature. After centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4 °C, the supernatants were collected and analyzed by Western blotting.

paper.abstract: Ependymal (E1) cells, with their tufts of ∼50 motile cilia, line the walls of the brain ventricles and help propel the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The CSF is rich in signaling molecules, but the cellular targets that detect these signals and their function remain unknown. Here, we describe a distinct population of ependymal cells (E2) in the forebrain of mice and humans, the majority having only 1 or 2 cilia. These cilia were motile, but unlike E1 cells' cilia, their pattern of motility and high expression of Arl13b and Inpp5e suggest a sensory function. E2 cells were characterized by an enormous, donut-like basal body that contained an increased number and size of subdistal appendages. In mice, E2 cells were mostly born in the embryo, but completed their differentiation in juveniles and young adults; they were found at higher densities in regions of high CSF flow and neurogenesis. E2 cilia contained the G protein-coupled receptor Smoothened, which accumulated in their cilia upon exposure to Sonic Hedgehog (Shh). Together, these findings identify E2 cells as a novel CSF-sensing ependymal cell type and provide a cellular target for the CSF signaling.

paper.title: Adropin signaling pathways in metabolic and non-metabolic disorders.
paper.abstract: Adropin is a secreted 76-amino-acid peptide encoded by the energy homeostasis-associated gene ENHO. First identified in 2008 as a nutrient-responsive signal linking macronutrient intake with energy balance and lipid metabolism, it is now recognized as a pleiotropic hormone with actions extending well beyond classical metabolic tissues. Circulating adropin is typically reduced in obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, atherosclerosis, heart failure, cognitive aging, and several fibrotic and reproductive disorders. However, diabetic kidney disease and some acute stress states show the opposite pattern. Two cell-surface partners, the orphan G-protein-coupled receptor GPR19 and the GPI-anchored neuronal protein NB-3/CNTN6, initiate overlapping but tissue-specific cascades: AMPK/ACC, PI3K/Akt/eNOS, GPR19/MAPK/PDK4, Notch1/Hes1, and TGF-β/GLI1. Through these pathways, adropin improves insulin action and mitochondrial fuel selection, increases endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability, restrains vascular remodeling, preserves blood-brain barrier integrity, and represses fibroblast activation. This review (i) separates metabolic from non-metabolic disease evidence, (ii) introduces an explicit evidence map distinguishing direct evidence, indirect evidence, and genuine controversy for every receptor and pathway, (iii) adds dedicated coverage of central feeding control, calcium-handling dysregulation in coronary disease, TGF-β/GLI1 signaling, biomarker interpretation, and translational pharmacology, and (iv) argues that progress now depends on receptor definition, assay harmonization, and delivery chemistry rather than on further disease associations. Remaining barriers include peptide instability, blood-brain-barrier delivery, non-standardized immunoassays, incomplete receptor pharmacology, and a narrow or bidirectional therapeutic window in kidney injury and tumor immunity.
